# Overview



This page is the entry point to the VCDesign-CED documentation. It explains what the project solves, how its two scoring routes differ, how the Candidate Effect Distillation (CED) pipeline fits together, and how the repository is organized — everything a first-time reader needs before running code or diving into the deep-dive chapters. No prior familiarity with the project is assumed; all claims below are traced to specific files so you can verify them yourself.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L38), [CODE_PACKAGE_README.md](CODE_PACKAGE_README.md#L1-L5)

## What Problem Does VCDesign Solve?

VCDesign addresses **cellular intervention design** — deciding which gene perturbation experiments are worth actually running. Instead of the usual machine learning framing of *predicting* a cell's response to a perturbation, VCDesign frames the task as **finite-budget ranking over a variable candidate set**: a solver ranks feasible interventions for a requested source-to-target cellular transition, and evaluation scores only the executable top-B prefix of that ranking using independently measured, held-out outcomes. In the benchmark shipped with this repository, the domain is CRISPRi Perturb-seq perturbations of human cell lines.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L32-L38), [CODE_PACKAGE_README.md](CODE_PACKAGE_README.md#L3-L9)

This framing produces three distinct capabilities, summarized below:

| Capability | What it means concretely |
| :--- | :--- |
| 🎯 **Rank a candidate set** | Score a variable set of feasible interventions for a source-to-target transition and select the top-B prefix. |
| 🧪 **Evaluate by outcomes** | Exclude the query identity and grade selected candidates using independently measured held-out outcomes — not by how well a model predicts them. |
| 🧬 **Transfer to unmeasured candidates** | Distill historical responses into an effect predictor that scores candidates whose responses were never measured, using STRING and MAP-KG knowledge features. |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L42-L59)

## Two Decision Routes: Retrieval or Prediction

A defining design choice of VCDesign is that it supports **two information regimes** at decision time. If a candidate's response has already been measured (e.g., in another cellular context), direct retrieval of that measured profile is available; if it has not, the predicted-effect route (VCDesign-CED) is used. Crucially, both routes feed the same downstream decision interface — a candidate pool, an experimental budget B, and outcome-based evaluation — so they remain directly comparable.

| Candidate information at decision time | Recommended route |
| :--- | :--- |
| Measured candidate responses are available | **Direct response-profile retrieval** |
| Candidate responses are unavailable | **VCDesign-CED predicted-effect scoring** |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L61-L68)

## Candidate Effect Distillation at a Glance

CED is the component that makes ranking possible for candidates whose responses were never measured. It learns a deliberately simple transfer map: historical perturbation responses are compressed into a **response basis** (a low-rank projection), STRING and MAP-KG candidate knowledge features drive a **ridge effect predictor** into that basis, and the reconstructed predicted effect is aligned against the requested target state. Two protocol guarantees matter for beginners: (1) the deployment candidate's measured response is **never an input** to CED — only knowledge features are; and (2) candidates missing all supported knowledge modalities receive a frozen "all-missing" score, so they are never silently dropped.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Historical perturbation responses"] --> B["Response basis<br/>(low-rank projection)"]
    B --> D["Ridge effect predictor"]
    C["STRING + MAP-KG<br/>candidate features"] --> D
    E["Unmeasured candidate<br/>(knowledge features only)"] --> D
    D --> F["Predicted effect vector"]
    F --> G["Target-alignment score"]
    G --> H["Fused with base scorer<br/>→ top-B ranking"]
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L111-L123), [examples/ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L17-L44)

> [!TIP]
> The architecture diagram above mirrors `examples/ced_demo.py` almost line for line — `basis.randomized_basis` builds the response basis, `RidgePath` is the predictor, `row_z` implements the fusion normalization. Running that 49-line file is the fastest way to see the whole pipeline execute end to end.

## Evaluation: Four Cellular Contexts

The benchmark spans four cellular contexts, all CRISPRi Perturb-seq. K562 serves as the primary genome-scale setting where the base scorer is trained, RPE1 provides cross-context evaluation, and HepG2 and Jurkat act as external cellular contexts that the model never adapts to. Data provenance — exact source versions and citations — is documented separately.

| Context | Perturbation setting | Role |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **K562** | CRISPRi Perturb-seq | Primary genome-scale setting |
| **RPE1** | CRISPRi Perturb-seq | Cross-context evaluation |
| **HepG2** | CRISPRi Perturb-seq | External cellular context |
| **Jurkat** | CRISPRi Perturb-seq | External cellular context |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L138-L147)

## What the Manuscript Establishes

The reported headline results are deliberately scoped. Under response masking in three held-out cellular contexts, CED delivers a **pooled paired BU@20 gain of +0.0492** over the same base scorer, and among 20 selections yields **1.11 more top-5% candidates** on average. When candidate responses have already been measured in other contexts, direct profile retrieval is stronger (**pooled BU@20 0.675 versus 0.508**). The authors are explicit that these are retrospective results for transcriptomic directional prioritization, not prospective evidence of improved biological endpoints — and that the fixed base scorer was itself trained on 68% of the masked candidate identities, with base-scorer-unseen subsets and a locked K562 identity test reported alongside.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L70-L76)

![VCDesign framework: finite-budget candidate ranking, outcome-based evaluation, and Candidate Effect Distillation for response-unseen deployment](https://github.com/Boom5426/VCDesign-CED/blob/main/assets/vcdesign_overview.png?raw=true)

## Repository Architecture

The codebase lives in a single Python package, `gene_open_inverse`, organized as **versioned protocol modules** — each directory suffixed `_v1` (or `_v2`) encapsulates one stage of the scientific workflow with its own `contract.py` defining data shapes and guarantees. This structure makes it possible to attribute every experimental number to exactly one module boundary. The overall data flow is:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph DATA["Data layer"]
        RESP["Measured responses<br/>four_context_v1"]
        KG["Knowledge features<br/>STRING + MAP-KG"]
    end
    subgraph SCORING["Scoring layer"]
        BASE["final_clean_model_v1<br/>base scorer"]
        CED["candidate_effect_distillation_v1<br/>basis → ridge → fusion"]
    end
    subgraph EVAL["Evaluation layer"]
        TOPB["Top-B selection"]
        METRICS["BU@B · MU@B · PHR@B<br/>evaluation_contract_v1"]
    end
    RESP --> BASE
    KG --> CED
    BASE --> TOPB
    CED --> TOPB
    TOPB --> METRICS
    EXT["external_baselines_v1<br/>GEARS · CellNavi · PHR"] --> METRICS
```

Sources: [PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md#L1-L17), [README.md](README.md#L196-L212)

The physical layout of the repository is compact — a source tree, one frozen configuration, a synthetic demo, and integrity tooling:

```text
VCDesign-CED/
├── src/gene_open_inverse/        versioned protocol modules (see tree below)
├── configs/paper_run_v1.json     frozen paper-run configuration + asset paths
├── examples/ced_demo.py          synthetic, data-free end-to-end CED demo
├── tools/                        SHA-256 release verification utilities
├── paper/VCDesign.pdf            manuscript
├── assets/                       framework overview figure and site assets
├── requirements.txt / -cpu.txt   exact pinned environments
└── pyproject.toml                package metadata, extras, pytest config
```

The main `src/gene_open_inverse` modules map to the workflow as follows:

| Module | Responsibility |
| :--- | :--- |
| `candidate_effect_distillation_v1` | CED basis, ridge predictor, score fusion, evaluation |
| `final_clean_model_v1` | Base scorer, checkpoint selection, locked evaluation |
| `four_context_v1` | K562 / RPE1 / HepG2 / Jurkat data contracts |
| `external_baselines_v1` | GEARS, CellNavi, PHR comparator adapters and reporting |
| `open_vocab_generalization_v1` | Response masking and open-vocabulary analyses |
| `revision_v1` | Gene-grouped ridge penalty selection (post-review default) |
| `model/` | Frozen knowledge features and model components |

Sources: [PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md#L4-L17), [README.md](README.md#L198-L212)

## Engineering Culture: Frozen Artifacts, Integrity, and Corrections

Three habits distinguish this repository and are worth internalizing before reading further. First, **everything large is frozen and verifiable**: processed inputs, checkpoints, and run records are released on a companion Hugging Face dataset with a `DATA_MANIFEST.json` containing byte sizes and SHA-256 digests, checked by `tools/verify_processed_data.py`. Second, **the experiment configuration is frozen**: `configs/paper_run_v1.json` pins asset paths, comparator checkpoints, and even the SHA-256 of the selected reference checkpoint (`final_clean_epoch_008.pt`), and the training entry point refuses to overwrite an existing output directory. Third, **the code is self-testing**: the expected protocol test result for this release is `169 passed` under `pytest`.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L149-L195), [CODE_PACKAGE_README.md](CODE_PACKAGE_README.md#L32-L45), [configs/paper_run_v1.json](configs/paper_run_v1.json#L1-L43)

> [!TIP]
> Watch the versioned module suffixes (`_v1`, `_v2`) throughout the source tree — they are not cosmetic. When a post-review correction changed ridge penalty selection from row-index CV to gene-grouped CV, it was added as `revision_v1` rather than silently patched, so the submitted and corrected implementations remain separately attributable. This "append, don't overwrite" pattern is why the SHA-256 manifests and test suite stay trustworthy.

Notably, two defects found during external review are documented rather than hidden: the ridge penalty selection was corrected to cut cross-validation folds by gene group (avoiding a gene leaking across folds), and the fusion normalization equation was restated to match what the code actually does — standardizing each branch over the whole scored pool. The originally submitted code is preserved unchanged in `release/VCDesign_ICLR2027_code/` for comparison, and the corrected protocol checks now fail under `pytest` when violated.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L125-L136)

## Your First Commands

Getting hands-on requires only Python 3.11 and no biological data. The bundled demo is fully synthetic — it checks response-basis construction, ridge effect prediction, missing-knowledge handling, and score fusion, and its scores are explicitly a software smoke test rather than a biological result. Note the optional-dependency design: the base install needs only NumPy, while `model` (PyTorch, SciPy), `data` (anndata, pandas, scikit-learn), and `dev` (pytest) extras are pulled in only when needed.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Boom5426/VCDesign-CED.git
cd VCDesign-CED
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e ".[model,data,dev]"
python examples/ced_demo.py
python -m pytest -q
```

| Install extra | Packages pulled in | Needed for |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| *(base)* | `numpy` | Package import only |
| `model` | `torch 2.4`, `scipy` | Base-scorer training and scoring |
| `data` | `anndata`, `pandas`, `scikit-learn` | Four-context data processing |
| `figures` | `matplotlib`, `scipy` | Plotting |
| `dev` | `pytest` | Protocol test suite |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L78-L109), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L29), [examples/ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L1-L5)

## Where to Go Next

The documentation is organized as a Get Started sequence followed by Deep Dive chapters. For the recommended beginner path: run the installation and smoke test first with [Quick Start](2-quick-start), then walk through the CED pipeline line by line in [Synthetic Demo Walkthrough](3-synthetic-demo-walkthrough), and only then attempt full reproduction with [Reproducing Paper Results](4-reproducing-paper-results) — which pairs with the data provenance details in [Data Sources and Provenance](5-data-sources-and-provenance). When you are ready for the internals, start at [Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview), then [Problem Formulation: Finite-Budget Ranking](7-problem-formulation-finite-budget-ranking) and the metric definitions in [Ranking Metrics: BU@B, MU@B, PHR@B](8-ranking-metrics-buatb-muatb-phratb), before working through the pipeline chapters [Response Basis Construction](11-response-basis-construction), [Ridge Effect Predictor](12-ridge-effect-predictor), and [Score Fusion and Beta Selection](14-score-fusion-and-beta-selection). For the integrity guarantees you saw summarized here, the dedicated chapters are [Leakage Prevention and Identity-Level Cross-Validation](21-leakage-prevention-and-identity-level-cross-validation), [Post-Review Corrections](22-post-review-corrections), and [Artifact Verification and SHA-256 Manifests](23-artifact-verification-and-sha-256-manifests).


# Quick Start



This page gets you from a fresh clone to a verified running VCDesign-CED environment in three commands. It covers prerequisites, environment installation, the bundled synthetic demo, and the protocol test suite — everything runs **without downloading biological data**. It does not cover paper-result reproduction or internal architecture; those follow in [Synthetic Demo Walkthrough](3-synthetic-demo-walkthrough) and [Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview).

![VCDesign framework overview](https://github.com/Boom5426/VCDesign-CED/blob/main/assets/vcdesign_overview.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L84-L95)

## Prerequisites

The only hard requirement is **Python 3.11** — the package explicitly declares `requires-python = ">=3.11,<3.12"`, so Python 3.10 or 3.12 will fail at install time. All core functionality builds on a deliberately small dependency surface: NumPy for arrays, SciPy and PyTorch for the model layer, plus anndata/pandas/scikit-learn for the data layer.

The optional dependency groups (install extras) control what you pull in:

| Extra | What it installs | Needed for Quick Start? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `model` | scipy, torch 2.4 | Yes — demo and tests import torch-backed scoring |
| `data` | anndata, pandas, scikit-learn | Yes — data-contract modules are imported by the test suite |
| `dev` | pytest 8.x | Yes — protocol test suite |
| `figures` | matplotlib, scipy | No — plotting only |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L10-L18), [requirements.txt](/requirements.txt#L1-L8)

## Step 1 — Clone and Install

The complete setup is a five-command sequence run from your terminal:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Boom5426/VCDesign-CED.git
cd VCDesign-CED
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e ".[model,data,dev]"
```

The `pip install -e .` **editable install** is what makes the `gene_open_inverse` package importable everywhere in the repo — the demo and tests never need `PYTHONPATH` tweaks, because setuptools discovers packages under `src/` and links them into your virtualenv in place.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["git clone repository"] --> B["python3.11 -m venv .venv"]
    B --> C["source .venv/bin/activate"]
    C --> D["pip install -e '.[model,data,dev]'"]
    D --> E{"Install succeeded?"}
    E -- "yes" --> F["Run synthetic demo"]
    E -- "no" --> X["Troubleshooting table below"]
    F --> G{"python examples/ced_demo.py<br/>prints ranked indices?"}
    G -- "yes" --> H["python -m pytest -q"]
    G -- "no" --> X
    H --> I{"All tests pass?"}
    I -- "yes" --> J["Environment verified ✔"]
    I -- "no" --> X
```

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L84-L92), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L25-L29)

> [!TIP]
> On Linux, the plain `torch` dependency resolves to the multi-gigabyte CUDA build by default. If you only want the CPU smoke test, use the pinned alternative: install `requirements-cpu.txt` first (it routes pip through PyTorch's CPU wheel index and fixes `torch==2.4.1`), then `pip install -e . --no-deps` to link the package without touching torch.

Sources: [requirements-cpu.txt](/requirements-cpu.txt#L1-L6), [README.md](/README.md#L98-L107)

## Step 2 — Run the Synthetic Demo

```bash
python examples/ced_demo.py
```

This 49-line script is the fastest way to confirm the CED pipeline is wired correctly. It generates a small synthetic world — 80 candidates, 64 training rows, 32 genes — with random STRING-like and MAP-KG-like knowledge features, then executes the full scoring path end to end. Two candidates are deliberately marked as missing all knowledge modalities so the demo can prove the **all-missing score** convention fires correctly.

The demo mirrors the real CED architecture: historical responses are compressed into a low-rank **response basis**, a **ridge effect predictor** trained on knowledge features projects unseen candidates onto that basis, and predicted effects are aligned against a goal vector and **fused** with a base-scorer output before ranking.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R["Synthetic responses<br/>80 × 32 matrix"] --> RB["Low-rank basis<br/>basis.randomized_basis(rank=8)"]
    RB --> T["Basis targets"]
    T --> RP["Ridge path<br/>predictor.RidgePath"]
    K["STRING + MAPKG features<br/>predictor.static_features"] --> RP
    RP --> E["Reconstructed effects<br/>basis.reconstruct"]
    E --> M["All-missing zeroing<br/>present_any mask"]
    G["Goal vector<br/>responses[train] normalized"] --> S["Directional score<br/>effect · goal"]
    B2["Base-scorer scores<br/>random illustrative"] --> F["Row-wise z fusion<br/>row_z + row_z"]
    S --> F
    M --> F
    F --> O["Ranked candidate indices<br/>(top 5 printed)"]
```

Expected output looks like:

```text
synthetic demo only; ranked candidate indices: [42, 7, 13, 55, 29]
all-missing raw effect scores: [0.0, 0.0]
```

Where the demo's steps map to the real source modules:

| Demo step | Module exercised | Source file |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Build knowledge features | `predictor.static_features` | `candidate_effect_distillation_v1/predictor.py` |
| Fit response basis | `basis.randomized_basis`, `.project`, `.reconstruct` | `candidate_effect_distillation_v1/basis.py` |
| Ridge prediction with penalty | `RidgePath(...).predict(penalty=1.0)` | `candidate_effect_distillation_v1/predictor.py` |
| All-missing handling | `features.present_any` mask → zero effect | `candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py` |
| Score fusion + ranking | `row_z` + `lexsort` | `final_clean_model_v1/scoring.py` |

Sources: [examples/ced_demo.py](/examples/ced_demo.py#L31-L46), [README.md](/README.md#L94-L95), [README.md](/README.md#L115-L123)

> **Note**: the demo's scores are a *software smoke test*, not a biological result — it validates that the response-basis construction, ridge effect prediction, missing-knowledge handling, and score fusion all execute without error.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L94-L95)

## Step 3 — Verify with the Protocol Test Suite

```bash
python -m pytest -q
```

The test suite covers the protocol guarantees across `src/gene_open_inverse` — this path is pre-configured in `pyproject.toml` as `testpaths`, so run pytest from the repository root (not from `src/`) or the configuration won't be discovered. Notably, the protocol checks in `revision_v1`, `external_baselines_v1`, and `open_vocab_generalization_v1` *fail under pytest* when their guarantees do not hold, so a green run is a meaningful integrity signal, not just an import check.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L28-L29), [README.md](/README.md#L163-L165)

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `pip install` rejects the environment | Python version ≠ 3.11 (package pins `>=3.11,<3.12`) | Ensure `python3.11` is on PATH; recreate the venv with it |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: gene_open_inverse` | Package not installed editable, or running from wrong venv | Re-run `pip install -e ".[model,data,dev]"` inside `.venv` |
| Install hangs downloading multi-GB CUDA libraries | Linux default `torch` wheel is the CUDA build | Use the CPU variant: `requirements-cpu.txt` + `pip install -e . --no-deps` |
| `pytest` collects nothing | Invoked from `src/` or a subdirectory, missing root config | Run `python -m pytest -q` from the repository root |
| Demo prints all-zero rankings for *all* candidates (not just last two) | Modified script or wrong install shadowing the package | Re-clone or reinstall; the demo prints zero only for the 2 all-missing candidates |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L10-L18), [requirements-cpu.txt](/requirements-cpu.txt#L1-L6)

## Your Position and Next Steps

At this point you have: a pinned Python 3.11 environment, an editable `vcdesign-ced` install, a passing synthetic CED demo, and a green protocol test suite. Nothing biological has been downloaded — the frozen Hugging Face dataset, checkpoint verification, and training commands belong to the reproduction flow, not the smoke test.

| Where to go next | Why |
| :--- | :--- |
| [Synthetic Demo Walkthrough](3-synthetic-demo-walkthrough) | Understand the demo you just ran, line by line |
| [Reproducing Paper Results](4-reproducing-paper-results) | Download frozen artifacts, verify SHA-256, train the base scorer |
| [Data Sources and Provenance](5-data-sources-and-provenance) | Where the K562/RPE1/HepG2/Jurkat inputs come from |
| [Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview) | How the `gene_open_inverse` modules fit together |

The repository's own entry-point map, for reference:

```text
src/gene_open_inverse/
├── candidate_effect_distillation_v1/  CED basis, predictor, fusion, evaluation
├── final_clean_model_v1/              final base scorer, selection, locked evaluation
├── four_context_v1/                   K562/RPE1/HepG2/Jurkat data contracts
├── external_baselines_v1/             comparator adapters and reporting
├── open_vocab_generalization_v1/      masking and open-vocabulary analyses
├── revision_v1/                       gene-grouped ridge penalty selection (the default)
└── model/                             frozen knowledge features and model components
configs/    portable asset paths and paper-run configuration
examples/   synthetic CED demonstration
tools/      processed-data SHA-256 verification
paper/      final manuscript PDF
```

Sources: [PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](/PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md#L1-L15), [configs/paper_run_v1.json](/configs/paper_run_v1.json#L1-L44), [README.md](/README.md#L84-L92)

> [!TIP]
> The frozen run contract `configs/paper_run_v1.json` already records the selected checkpoint's SHA-256 and every input asset path — when you later move to [Reproducing Paper Results](4-reproducing-paper-results), this file is the single source of truth that `tools/verify_processed_data.py` checks every released byte against, so never edit it manually.

# Synthetic Demo Walkthrough



This page walks you, step by step, through `examples/ced_demo.py` — the bundled synthetic smoke test for VCDesign-CED. The demo exercises the full Candidate Effect Distillation (CED) deployment path using nothing but random NumPy data: no downloads, no GPU, no biological inputs, and no biological conclusions. If the demo runs and prints its two expected lines, the core scoring machinery is wired correctly on your machine.

![VCDesign framework overview](https://github.com/Boom5426/VCDesign-CED/blob/main/assets/vcdesign_overview.png?raw=true)

Sources: [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L1-L2), [README.md](README.md#L94-L95)

## What the Demo Is — and What It Is Not

The demo's own docstring sets the scope: it is a *"small synthetic VCDesign-CED smoke example; no biological result is reported."* The repository README is equally explicit — the demo *"checks response-basis construction, ridge effect prediction, missing-knowledge handling, and score fusion. Its scores are a software smoke test, not a biological result."* In the reproduction guide it sits at step 2, "Run software checks," immediately before `pytest`. Treat its printed ranking the way you treat a unit test assertion: evidence that code executes correctly, not evidence about cells.

Sources: [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L2), [README.md](README.md#L82-L95), [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L19-L24)

## Prerequisites and How to Run It

The only hard requirement is **Python 3.11** — the package pins `requires-python = ">=3.11,<3.12"` and depends on `numpy>=1.26,<2`, which is all the demo itself needs. The recommended quick start installs the editable package with the `model`, `data`, and `dev` extras, then runs the demo and the test suite:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Boom5426/VCDesign-CED.git
cd VCDesign-CED
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e ".[model,data,dev]"
python examples/ced_demo.py
python -m pytest -q
```

| Requirement | Detail | Verified in |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Python version | 3.11 only (`>=3.11,<3.12`) | [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L10) |
| Core dependency | `numpy>=1.26,<2` (demo needs nothing else) | [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L11) |
| Install command | `pip install -e ".[model,data,dev]"` | [README.md](README.md#L84-L92) |
| Run command | `python examples/ced_demo.py` | [README.md](README.md#L84-L92), [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L22-L24) |
| CPU-only alternative | `pip install -r requirements-cpu.txt` then `pip install -e . --no-deps` | [README.md](README.md#L100-L105) |

If something goes wrong, the usual suspects are version drift and a missing editable install:

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `ModuleNotFoundError: gene_open_inverse` | Package not installed in editable mode | Re-run `python -m pip install -e ".[model,data,dev]"` from the repo root |
| NumPy 2.x API errors | Environment resolved NumPy outside the pin | Recreate the venv with Python 3.11 and reinstall |
| Syntax errors on `dict[str, np.ndarray]` hints | Python < 3.11 despite `from __future__ import annotations` extras | Install Python 3.11; the project refuses other versions |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L10-L18), [README.md](README.md#L80-L109), [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L19-L24)

## The Pipeline at a Glance

The demo is 49 lines, and every line maps to one stage of the production CED pipeline. Here is the complete flow before we dissect each stage:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["① Synthetic world<br/>rng(7): 80 candidates × 32 genes<br/>5-dim shared latent"] --> B["② Role stand-in<br/>STRING 80×12 + MAPKG 80×10<br/>last 2 candidates flagged all-missing"]
    B --> C["③ static_features()<br/>zero-filled blocks + present flags"]
    A --> D["④ randomized_basis(responses[:64], rank=8)<br/>sketch → QR → power iterations → SVD"]
    D --> E["⑤ project() → basis coefficients<br/>= ridge targets in z-space"]
    C --> E
    E --> F["⑥ RidgePath(features[:64], targets)<br/>standardize features → one SVD"]
    F --> G["⑦ predict(penalty=1.0) on rows 64–79<br/>reconstruct() back to gene space"]
    G --> H["⑧ Zero effects for all-missing candidates<br/>(contract: ALL_MISSING_SCORE = 0.0)"]
    H --> I["⑨ Cosine to goal + row_z fusion<br/>with illustrative base score"]
    I --> J["⑩ lexsort ranking → print top-5<br/>+ all-missing raw scores"]
```

Sources: [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L17-L44)

## Step 1–2: Building the Synthetic World

The demo constructs a miniature universe in which the knowledge→effect signal is guaranteed to exist. A seeded generator (`np.random.default_rng(7)`) draws a 5-dimensional latent vector for each of 80 candidates. Responses (80 × 32 genes) and both knowledge modalities — STRING (80 × 12 features) and MAPKG (80 × 10 features) — are generated as *linear maps of the same latent*. This is the crucial design decision: because candidate knowledge and candidate responses share a latent cause, a linear map from knowledge to effect **must** be learnable, which makes the demo a positive control for the ridge stage rather than a random-noise sanity check.

The `Role` class is a minimal stand-in for the production role-array objects: it carries exactly the two dictionaries that `predictor.static_features` expects — `capabilities` (feature matrices per modality) and `capability_present` (boolean flags). Two candidates — the last two rows — get their knowledge flags set to `False` in every modality, creating the all-missing case the contract explicitly legislates for.

Sources: [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L11-L28), [scoring.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/scoring.py#L73-L92)

## Step 3: Static Feature Assembly

`predictor.static_features(role, contract.PRIMARY_MODALITIES)` converts the role into a single modeling matrix. For each modality named in the contract (`PRIMARY_MODALITIES = ("STRING", "MAPKG")`), it takes the descriptor block, **zeroes out every row whose knowledge is not present**, and appends a 0/1 present-flag column per modality. The returned `StaticFeatures` carries three things: `values` (the concatenated matrix), `present_any` (at least one modality available per candidate), and `names`. This zero-fill-plus-flag encoding is exactly how the production pipeline feeds knowledge to both the ridge and the base scorer — the demo is not a simplification here.

Sources: [predictor.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/predictor.py#L33-L43), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L41)

## Step 4: Response Basis Construction

`basis.randomized_basis(responses[:train_count], rank=8)` computes the response basis `B` from the 64 training responses only. The function sketches the response matrix with `rank + 32` random projections (the +32 is `BASIS_OVERSAMPLE`), QR-factorizes the sketch, runs 4 power iterations (`BASIS_POWER_ITERATIONS`), and finally takes the top-`rank` right singular vectors of the reduced matrix. The result is a frozen `ResponseBasis` dataclass holding `basis`, `singular_values`, and `total_energy`, with an `.explained` property reporting the fraction of response energy captured.

Two protocol details survive into the demo unchanged: the basis is computed **uncentered** — the module docstring explains that `B` spans the response space itself, not deviations from the mean, so `r_hat = B z_hat` is a complete reconstruction rather than an offset — and the seed defaults to the frozen production constant `BASIS_SEED = 20260918`. Only the rank is shrunk (8 here versus `BASIS_RANK = 256` in production, where genes number 8,248 rather than 32).

Sources: [basis.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/basis.py#L58-L75), [basis.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/basis.py#L1-L9), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L50-L55)

## Step 5–7: Ridge Prediction and Reconstruction

The next four lines are the heart of CED. First, `fitted_basis.project(responses[:64])` maps each training response into basis coordinates — these coefficients are the ridge's regression targets in "z-space." Second, `RidgePath(features.values[:64], targets)` is constructed: it standardizes the features (per-column mean and standard deviation, with a 1e-8 floor), centers the targets, and takes **one SVD** — the class docstring calls this "One SVD, every penalty for free," because any ridge penalty's weights can be recovered from the stored SVD without refitting.

Third, `path.predict(features.values[train_count:], penalty=1.0)` predicts basis coefficients for the 16 held-out candidates, and `fitted_basis.reconstruct(...)` maps those coefficients back to full 32-gene effects. Fourth — and this is the missing-knowledge contract in action — `effect[~features.present_any[train_count:]] = 0.0` sets the predicted effect of any candidate with no knowledge modality to exactly zero. The contract is unambiguous about why: *"A candidate with no static modality present has no predicted effect. It is given an exactly neutral score rather than a learned one... Neutral means zero: a cosine's own indifference point, fixed here and not tuned."*

> [!TIP]
> The demo sequence — project → fit `RidgePath` on fit rows → predict → reconstruct → zero missing rows — is a line-for-line miniature of `FrozenEffectPredictor` in `final_clean_model_v1/scoring.py`, the object that produces the paper's actual effect predictions. Learn the demo and you have learned the real deployment path end to end.

Sources: [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L31-L35), [predictor.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/predictor.py#L46-L63), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L30-L36), [scoring.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/scoring.py#L73-L89)

## Step 8–9: Scoring, Fusion, and Ranking

Scoring works in the gene space where effects live. The demo takes the first scored candidate's response as the "goal," normalizes it, and computes an **effect score** for every candidate: the cosine between the candidate's predicted effect and the goal direction (norms floored at 1e-30 to protect the zeroed all-missing rows). This mirrors `SCORE_NAME = "PREDICTED_EFFECT_COSINE"` from the frozen contract.

A **base score** is then drawn from a random normal distribution — explicitly commented as an *"illustrative scorer output"* — standing in for the trained neural base scorer used in production. Fusion is the same per-row standardization the manuscript uses: `row_z(base_score) + row_z(effect_score)`, where `row_z` subtracts the row mean and divides by the row standard deviation (floored at 1e-12). The README's post-review correction notes confirm this semantic — *"the two branches are standardized per query row over every column they are given."* Finally, `np.lexsort` ranks candidates by descending fused score, with the original index as a deterministic tie-breaker, and prints the top five.

Sources: [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L37-L43), [scoring.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/scoring.py#L112-L115), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L70-L76), [README.md](README.md#L125-L132)

## Reading the Output

The demo prints exactly two lines, and each is a pass/fail signal:

```text
synthetic demo only; ranked candidate indices: [ ... ]   # top-5 by fused score
all-missing raw effect scores: [0.0, 0.0]                # the missing-knowledge contract held
```

The second line is the one that matters for protocol integrity: candidates 78 and 79 were flagged as missing all knowledge, their effects were zeroed, and their raw cosine scores must therefore be exactly `0.0` — the frozen `ALL_MISSING_SCORE`. If you ever see non-zero values there, the missing-knowledge path has regressed.

Sources: [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L26-L28), [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L35), [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L43-L44), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L71)

## Demo versus Production: a Precise Comparison

The demo compresses the production pipeline deliberately. This table tells you exactly which simplifications to unlearn before reading the deep-dive pages:

| Aspect | Synthetic demo | Production pipeline |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Data | 80 × 32 synthetic latent-linear responses | Real CRISPRi Perturb-seq, 8,248 genes, four contexts |
| Basis rank | 8 (passed explicitly) | `BASIS_RANK = 256`, frozen in advance |
| Basis seed | Default → `BASIS_SEED = 20260918` (same) | Same frozen constant |
| Data split | First 64 rows fit, last 16 scored (row split, for brevity) | Identity-level cross-validation; queries disjoint from supervision |
| Penalty | Fixed at 1.0 | Chosen from `RIDGE_PENALTIES` by 5-fold identity CV on held-out cosine |
| Base score | `rng.normal` placeholder | Trained neural base scorer (`final_clean_model_v1`) |
| Goal vector | One held-out candidate's response | Query-defined source-to-target transition `d_q` |
| Fusion call | Manual `row_z(a) + row_z(b)` | `four_context_v1.evaluate.fuse` with `standardize_over` masks |
| Output meaning | Smoke test only | Reported BU@B / MU@B / PHR@B benchmark numbers |

> [!TIP]
> The synthetic world is engineered so knowledge and responses share a latent cause — that is why the linear ridge *succeeds* in the demo. In production, whether a linear knowledge→effect map carries enough signal is precisely the empirical question the paper answers, so do not extrapolate the demo's clean result to real-data expectations.

Sources: [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L18-L42), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L50-L68), [predictor.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/predictor.py#L66-L110), [scoring.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/scoring.py#L73-L109), [README.md](README.md#L128-L132)

## Where You Are in the Codebase

Only these four source files participate in the demo; everything else in `src/gene_open_inverse/` belongs to training, evaluation, or baseline stages you will meet later:

```text
examples/
└── ced_demo.py                          ← the walkthrough subject
src/gene_open_inverse/
├── candidate_effect_distillation_v1/
│   ├── basis.py                         ← randomized_basis, ResponseBasis
│   ├── predictor.py                     ← static_features, RidgePath
│   └── contract.py                      ← PRIMARY_MODALITIES, frozen constants
└── final_clean_model_v1/
    └── scoring.py                       ← row_z, FrozenEffectPredictor (production twin)
```

Sources: [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L7-L8), [PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md)

## Where to Go Next

You have now traced the complete CED deployment path in miniature. The natural progression from here:

- Run the real thing next: [Reproducing Paper Results](4-reproducing-paper-results) covers frozen-data download, SHA-256 verification, and the training command.
- Going backwards for context: [Overview](1-overview) frames the finite-budget ranking problem, and [Quick Start](2-quick-start) is the condensed version of the setup shown here.
- Deep dives on the three stages you just saw: [Response Basis Construction](11-response-basis-construction) for the uncentered randomized SVD, [Ridge Effect Predictor](12-ridge-effect-predictor) for identity-level cross-validation and penalty selection, and [Score Fusion and Beta Selection](14-score-fusion-and-beta-selection) for how `row_z` fusion extends into the evaluated protocol.


# Reproducing Paper Results



This page is the operational counterpart to the manuscript: it walks through the canonical command sequence that turns a fresh clone into a verified, paper-faithful result. Reproduction here has two tiers. **Tier one** is byte-level verification of the frozen release — you download the processed inputs, checkpoints, and run records from the companion Hugging Face dataset and prove every byte matches its SHA-256 manifest. **Tier two** is re-execution — you retrain the primary base scorer under the frozen recipe and compare against the released records. Every command runs from the repository root, and the long-running stages refuse to overwrite an existing output directory by design.

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L1-L4), [README.md](README.md#L166-L186)

![VCDesign framework overview](https://github.com/Boom5426/VCDesign-CED/blob/main/assets/vcdesign_overview.png?raw=true)

## The Full Reproduction Sequence at a Glance

The workflow is a strictly ordered chain where each stage gates the next: integrity is proven before any code executes, software sanity is checked before any GPU time is spent, and a configuration lock is written before the evaluation split is touched. The following flowchart shows both the commands you run and the phase modules they invoke:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Clone repo<br>Python 3.11 venv"] --> B["pip install -e . plus extras<br>and huggingface_hub"]
    B --> C["hf download Boom5426/VCDesign<br>inputs, checkpoints, records, manifest"]
    C --> D{"tools/verify_processed_data.py"}
    D -- "any FAIL line" --> X["Stop: byte integrity failed"]
    D -- "all files verified" --> E["examples/ced_demo.py smoke test"]
    E --> F["pytest -q"]
    F --> G["Phase D: final_clean_model_v1.train"]
    G --> H["epoch checkpoints + train_manifest.json"]
    H --> I["Phase E: select.py<br>one checkpoint per arm on G_select"]
    I --> J["Phase F: lock.py<br>pre-evaluation lock record"]
    J --> K["Phase G: gcheck.py<br>the one locked evaluation on G_check"]
    K --> L["Compare with paper and records/"]
    style X fill:#fde8e8
```

The **verify-first ordering** is not stylistic: the verifier's exit code is 1 whenever any file fails, so a corrupt or partial download fails loudly before training begins.

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L3-L13), [tools/verify_processed_data.py](tools/verify_processed_data.py#L45-L52)

## Step 1 — Set Up the Environment

The package pins **Python 3.11 exactly** (`requires-python = ">=3.11,<3.12"`) and is installed in editable mode with three extras: `model` (scipy and torch), `data` (anndata, pandas, scikit-learn), and `dev` (pytest). The reproduction guide additionally pins `huggingface_hub>=0.35` for the `hf` download CLI used in step 2.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L10-L18), [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L8-L12), [README.md](README.md#L82)

Two ready-made dependency files serve different hardware targets, and choosing between them is the first real decision of the run:

| Install path | Contents | Intended use |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `pip install -e ".[model,data,dev]"` | Range-pinned extras; torch ≥2.4,<2.5 | GPU training run |
| `requirements.txt` | Exact pins: numpy 1.26.4, scipy 1.15.1, anndata 0.11.3, pandas 1.5.3, scikit-learn 1.5.2, matplotlib 3.9.2, pytest 8.3.5 | Pinned stack (no torch) |
| `requirements-cpu.txt` | `requirements.txt` + torch 2.4.1 from the PyTorch CPU wheel index | CPU verification without gigabytes of CUDA libraries |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L14-L18), [requirements.txt](requirements.txt#L1-L7), [requirements-cpu.txt](requirements-cpu.txt#L1-L5)

For a GPU training run, install the PyTorch 2.4 build appropriate for your local CUDA system, then the remaining pins from `requirements.txt`. For CPU-only verification, `requirements-cpu.txt` points pip at the CPU wheel index explicitly, because without it pip on Linux installs the CUDA build and several gigabytes of GPU libraries the CPU verification never uses.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L100-L108), [requirements-cpu.txt](requirements-cpu.txt#L2-L5)

## Step 2 — Download and Verify the Frozen Snapshot

GitHub hosts only source, configuration, the synthetic demo, and the manuscript. The large processed artifacts live in the companion dataset `Boom5426/VCDesign` on Hugging Face and are pulled selectively into the repository root:

```bash
hf download Boom5426/VCDesign --repo-type dataset --local-dir . \
  --include 'inputs/**' 'checkpoints/**' 'records/**' 'DATA_MANIFEST.json'
```

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L10-L13), [README.md](README.md#L214-L215)

Each downloaded directory plays a distinct role in the reproduction story:

| Released artifact | Contents |
| :--- | :--- |
| `inputs/` | Frozen response, STRING, MAP-KG, candidate-knowledge, and comparator arrays |
| `checkpoints/` | The selected epoch-8 reference checkpoint |
| `records/` | Training, selection, evaluation, external-baseline, and verification records |
| `DATA_MANIFEST.json` | Byte sizes and SHA-256 digests for release verification |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L157-L162)

Verification is a single command: `python3 tools/verify_processed_data.py --root .`. The tool is deliberately strict, and its checks are worth understanding because each failure mode maps to a different root cause. It first validates the manifest itself — schema must be `VCDESIGN_PROCESSED_DATA_V1`, and every path must be relative, non-traversing, and unique. It then walks every entry, rejecting symlinks, checking the byte size, and finally hashing each file with a streaming 16 MiB-block SHA-256.

Sources: [tools/verify_processed_data.py](tools/verify_processed_data.py#L26-L44), [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L16-L17)

The manifest covers records whose compute-host paths were replaced by relative release paths, so what you verify is exactly what the paper's runs consumed. A clean run prints `verified N/N processed-data files` and exits 0; any failure prints a `FAIL` line per problem and exits 1.

> [!TIP]
> The verifier's rejection of symlinks and absolute paths is a supply-chain guard, not a convenience: it guarantees that the tree you hash is a plain, self-contained snapshot rather than a view onto other storage that could change underneath the digest.

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L16-L17), [tools/verify_processed_data.py](tools/verify_processed_data.py#L33-L44)

## Step 3 — Software Sanity Checks

Two commands establish that the installed code is healthy before any expensive stage runs. First, `python3 examples/ced_demo.py` executes a small synthetic end-to-end smoke example — randomized response basis, ridge effect prediction, missing-knowledge handling, and score fusion — built entirely from `numpy` random data with no biological inputs. Its docstring is explicit that no biological result is reported; the printed ranked indices are a software check only. Second, `python3 -m pytest -q` runs the protocol test suite, which pytest discovers under `src/gene_open_inverse` as configured in `pyproject.toml`.

Sources: [examples/ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L1-L2), [examples/ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L17-L44), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L28-L29), [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L19-L24)

## Step 4 — Retrain the Primary Base Scorer (Phase D)

The one documented re-execution command is:

```bash
python3 -m gene_open_inverse.final_clean_model_v1.train \
  --config configs/paper_run_v1.json \
  --output outputs/final_clean_train \
  --device cuda
```

It requires a CUDA device and an **empty output path** — `run()` calls `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=False)`, so an existing directory aborts immediately. This refusal is a deliberate audit property: a second, adjusted run cannot quietly replace the first.

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L28-L35), [train.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/train.py#L44-L45)

> [!TIP]
> The training recipe is *imported, not reimplemented*: `_epoch`, `_role_tensors`, `_seed`, `capture_branch_state`, and every constant (seed, learning rate, weight decay, clip norm, batch size, objective schedule) come directly from the incumbent training module `global_objective_knowledge_attribution_v1.train_factorial`. Optimizer, scheduler, loss, sampler, and seeds are therefore identical to the paper's recipe by construction rather than by inspection — the only two deltas are the strict-legal modality set without TEXT and the removal of the learnable unknown token.

Sources: [train.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/train.py#L2-L19), [train.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/train.py#L54-L65)

Internally, the run enforces its legality contract twice: the frozen loader loads STRING+MAPKG+TEXT exactly as frozen and then drops TEXT before any tensor exists, raising if TEXT ever reaches a training tensor; and the model must not carry a parameter ending in `unknown_token`. Epochs alternate PAIR-then-SET objectives, and from the branch phase onward every epoch checkpoint is saved with its own SHA-256.

Sources: [train.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/train.py#L47-L61), [train.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/train.py#L69-L86)

The run writes per-epoch checkpoints plus `train_manifest.json`, a self-describing record containing the recipe (with its source module), modality dimensions, parameter count, full loss history, checkpoint digests, and a runtime block capturing timestamp, Python version, and torch version. This is what lets a retrained run be compared field-by-field against the released record in `records/`.

Sources: [train.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/train.py#L88-L109), [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L37-L39)

## Step 5 — Selection, Lock, and the Locked Evaluation (Phases E–G)

Training alone does not produce the paper numbers. The remaining chain is a three-phase discipline encoded in `final_clean_model_v1`, and its shape matters for anyone auditing the result:

| Phase | Module | Decides | Reads `G_check`? | Writes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| E — Select | `select.py` | One checkpoint per arm, on `G_select` only | No | Selection record |
| F — Lock | `lock.py` | Nothing — freezes everything hashed | No | `VCDESIGN_FINAL_LOCK_V1` + `lock_sha256` |
| G — Evaluate | `gcheck.py` | Nothing — the one locked final evaluation | Yes, via acknowledgement-gated loader | Locked evaluation record |

Sources: [select.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/select.py#L2-L8), [lock.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/lock.py#L2-L8), [gcheck.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/gcheck.py#L2-L17)

Phase F hashes not only artifacts but **the code itself**: every `.py` file in the four evaluation-relevant packages is digested, because a commit hash alone could not identify the code that produced the lock. After the lock exists, no configuration change is permitted, and the evaluation module reads its checkpoints and predictor penalty from that record.

Sources: [lock.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/lock.py#L30-L46), [lock.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/lock.py#L57-L65)

Every phase that touches the effect predictor verifies it against the frozen artifact first: the rebuilt `FrozenEffectPredictor` must reproduce the released `predicted_effect_G_select.npy` within a max absolute difference of 1e-3, or the phase aborts. The locked evaluation itself refuses to overwrite its own output, and `gcheck.py` is the only module in the repository that reaches the `G_check` split — through `locked_check_arrays`, which refuses to run without an explicit acknowledgement string.

Sources: [select.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/select.py#L57-L67), [gcheck.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/gcheck.py#L59-L61), [gcheck.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/gcheck.py#L79-L86)

The evaluation scores seven rows under declared legality labels — `RANDOM`, `STRICT_LEGAL_CANDIDATE_PRIOR`, `EFFECT_BRANCH_ONLY`, `LEGACY_M_SET` (context only, not the paired comparator), `CLEAN_BASE`, `CLEAN_EFFECT`, and the diagnostic `MEASURED_RESPONSE_ORACLE` — then reports paired bootstrap comparisons, with `CLEAN_EFFECT minus CLEAN_BASE` as the primary causal contrast. For most reproduction purposes you will not re-run Phases E–G: the released `records/` already contain the selection, lock, and evaluation records, and their digests are covered by the manifest you verified in step 2.

Sources: [gcheck.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/gcheck.py#L47-L55), [gcheck.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/gcheck.py#L172-L180), [README.md](README.md#L157-L162)

## Step 6 — Compare Against the Manuscript

The frozen run contract is `configs/paper_run_v1.json` (schema `VCDESIGN_PAPER_RUN_V1`). It is the single anchor point binding the paper to bytes on disk, and three fields matter most when checking your retrained output against the release:

| Config field | Value | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `checkpoints.FINAL_CLEAN_EPOCH_008` | `checkpoints/final_clean_epoch_008.pt`, epoch 8 | Selected for CLEAN_BASE and CLEAN_EFFECT |
| `checkpoints.M_PAIR` / `M_SET` | `inputs/comparators/*_epoch_010.pt` | Frozen GOKA final-config endpoints at epoch 10 |
| `selected_checkpoint_sha256` | `58da13d252faf9bcaa74c53345c0afc380882bdd5f410a77cfa5044f9a6e9484` | SHA-256 of the frozen reference checkpoint |
| `cached_scores` | Five comparator score arrays | Frozen retrieval and comparator scores |
| `data_manifest` | `DATA_MANIFEST.json` | The verified release manifest |

Sources: [configs/paper_run_v1.json](configs/paper_run_v1.json#L17-L42), [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L37-L39)

The paper itself — [paper/VCDesign.pdf](paper/VCDesign.pdf) — defines the candidate pools, evaluation protocol, comparator settings, and reported results, and raw H5AD matrices can be obtained from the public sources catalogued in [DATA_SOURCES.md](DATA_SOURCES.md). As a spot-check of a successful re-run, the headline expectations are: a pooled paired BU@20 gain of `+0.0492` over the same base scorer under response masking, `1.11` more top-5% candidates among 20 selections on average, and direct profile retrieval scoring higher than VCDesign-CED when candidate responses exist in other contexts (pooled BU@20 `0.675` vs `0.508`). Full metric definitions and interpretation belong on the dedicated pages.

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L41-L46), [README.md](README.md#L72-L74)

## Troubleshooting

Each strictness rule in the pipeline produces a specific, diagnosable failure message:

| Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `unrecognized processed-data manifest schema` | `DATA_MANIFEST.json` is not the expected `VCDESIGN_PROCESSED_DATA_V1` | Re-download the snapshot; do not hand-edit the manifest |
| `size mismatch` / `SHA-256 mismatch: <path>` | Partial or corrupted download | Delete affected files, re-run `hf download`, re-verify |
| `missing or symlink: <path>` | Incomplete download, or a symlinked file | Re-download; the verifier rejects symlinks outright |
| `invalid or duplicate manifest path` | Tampered or wrong-version manifest | Restore the released `DATA_MANIFEST.json` |
| `FileExistsError` at training start | `--output` directory already exists | Supply a new, empty output path (by design, no overwrite) |
| `TEXT reached a training tensor` / strict-modality `RuntimeError` | Modified config or tampered module | Use `configs/paper_run_v1.json` unmodified |
| `the effect predictor is not the locked one` (or the Phase E equivalent, `> 1e-3`) | Distillation inputs differ from release | Re-verify the snapshot; check the penalty in `candidate_effect_distillation.json` |
| `refuses to overwrite` (lock or evaluation) | Re-running Phase F/G into the same output | Use a fresh output path; the refusal is the audit mechanism |

Sources: [tools/verify_processed_data.py](tools/verify_processed_data.py#L26-L44), [train.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/train.py#L44-L58), [select.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/select.py#L63-L67), [lock.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/lock.py#L57-L60), [gcheck.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/gcheck.py#L59-L61), [gcheck.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/gcheck.py#L83-L86)

## Where to Go Next

A natural progression from here: if you want the synthetic pipeline mechanics without any data download, work through [Synthetic Demo Walkthrough](3-synthetic-demo-walkthrough); for the upstream provenance of every raw matrix behind `DATA_SOURCES.md`, see [Data Sources and Provenance](5-data-sources-and-provenance). To go deeper on the machinery referenced above, [Artifact Verification and SHA-256 Manifests](23-artifact-verification-and-sha-256-manifests) expands on step 2, [Training Pipeline and Frozen Configuration](16-training-pipeline-and-frozen-configuration) expands on steps 4–5, and [Protocol Test Suite](24-protocol-test-suite) details what `pytest -q` actually checks. Finally, to interpret the numbers you reproduced, continue to [Key Benchmark Findings](26-key-benchmark-findings).


# Data Sources and Provenance



Every number a VCDesign-CED experiment produces is ultimately a deterministic function of a small set of *public* biological datasets plus frozen code. This page explains exactly which public resources the project is built from, how the project records *which bytes* of those resources it used, and how you can verify — byte by byte — that the processed snapshot on your machine is identical to the one used for the paper. If you have followed [Reproducing Paper Results](4-reproducing-paper-results), this page explains the "why" behind the `hf download` and verification commands you already ran.

Sources: [DATA_SOURCES.md](DATA_SOURCES.md#L1-L18), [CODE_PACKAGE_README.md](CODE_PACKAGE_README.md#L82-L84)

## Two Layers of Data in This Project

VCDesign-CED deliberately separates *code* from *data*. The repository you are browsing contains the Python source tree, the frozen paper-run configuration, a synthetic smoke-test demo, and verification tooling — but explicitly **no raw H5AD matrices, no large processed inputs, no checkpoints, and no cached run records**. Those heavyweight artifacts live in a companion processed-data release on Hugging Face (`Boom5426/VCDesign`), which you download alongside the code.

Sources: [CODE_PACKAGE_README.md](CODE_PACKAGE_README.md#L11-L30), [README.md](README.md#L149-L162)

![VCDesign overview](https://github.com/Boom5426/VCDesign-CED/blob/main/assets/vcdesign_overview.png?raw=true)

The released artifact set has exactly four top-level entries, each with a defined role:

| Released artifact | Contents |
| :--- | :--- |
| `inputs/` | Frozen response matrices, STRING features, MAP-KG features, candidate-knowledge arrays, and comparator score arrays |
| `checkpoints/` | The selected epoch-8 reference checkpoint (`final_clean_epoch_008.pt`) |
| `records/` | Training, selection, evaluation, external-baseline, and verification run records |
| `DATA_MANIFEST.json` | Byte sizes and SHA-256 digests for every released file |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L149-L162)

## The Public Data Sources

The processed release is derived from six public resources, each feeding a specific part of the pipeline. The two single-cell perturbation datasets provide the measured gene-expression responses; the remaining four provide *knowledge features* — static biological information about genes that the effect predictor consumes (this is explored in [Knowledge Features: STRING and MAP-KG](13-knowledge-features-string-and-map-kg)).

| Resource | Use in VCDesign-CED |
| :--- | :--- |
| Replogle et al. Perturb-seq release (figshare) | K562 genome-scale and RPE1 essential CRISPRi screens |
| GEO GSE264667 | HepG2 and Jurkat CRISPRi screens |
| STRING v12.0 | Static protein interaction features |
| MAP and MAP-KG | Frozen knowledge-graph gene representation |
| ESM-2 | Protein sequence representation |
| Reactome release 97 + NCBI human Gene Info | Pathway and gene-description feature variants |

Sources: [DATA_SOURCES.md](DATA_SOURCES.md#L1-L18)

The four single-cell datasets map onto the four evaluation *cellular contexts*, each with a distinct role in the benchmark. All four share the same perturbation setting: gene-level CRISPRi knockdown, dual-sgRNA, day 7, measured on the 10x 3' v3 platform — this uniformity is what makes cross-context comparison meaningful.

| Context | Role |
| :--- | :--- |
| K562 | Primary genome-scale setting (the "anchor" context) |
| RPE1 | Cross-context evaluation |
| HepG2 | External cellular context |
| Jurkat | External cellular context |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L138-L147), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L56-L65)

## Why the Right K562 Screen Matters

A single subtlety worth flagging for beginners: the Replogle release contains *two* K562 datasets — a **genome-scale** screen and an **essentialome** screen. VCDesign-CED uses the **K562 genome-scale** screen only, because it is the genome-scale screen that defines the candidate universe for the primary setup. Downloading the wrong K562 file would silently give you a different (smaller) candidate pool and numbers that do not match the paper. The canonical URLs in `DATA_SOURCES.md` are the authoritative reference.

Sources: [DATA_SOURCES.md](DATA_SOURCES.md#L15-L18)

## The Provenance Chain: From Raw Bytes to Verified Release

Provenance in this project is not a README paragraph — it is a *pipeline stage*. The raw GEO H5AD files are the only external inputs the four-context mission takes, and everything downstream is a deterministic function of those bytes plus frozen code. The workflow below shows how public bytes become verified artifacts on your machine:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph PUB["Public sources"]
        G["GEO GSE264667<br/>HepG2 + Jurkat raw H5AD"]
        R["Replogle figshare release<br/>K562 + RPE1"]
    end
    subgraph PIPE["Provenance pipeline"]
        P0["Phase 0: manifest.py<br/>asset manifest = provenance root<br/>URL · timestamp · bytes · SHA-256<br/>+ server-advertised size cross-check"]
        P2["Phase 2: build.py<br/>frozen measurement contract<br/>'trains nothing and ranks nothing'"]
        DOC["dataset_doc.py<br/>audit doc regenerated from JSON<br/>so numbers cannot drift"]
    end
    subgraph REL["Hugging Face release"]
        IN["inputs/"]
        CK["checkpoints/"]
        REC["records/"]
        DM["DATA_MANIFEST.json<br/>size + SHA-256 per file"]
    end
    subgraph YOU["Your machine"]
        DL["hf download Boom5426/VCDesign"]
        VF["tools/verify_processed_data.py<br/>schema · path · size · SHA-256"]
        RUN["training / evaluation"]
    end
    G --> P0 --> P2
    R --> P2
    P2 --> IN
    P2 --> REC
    P2 --> DOC
    IN --> DL
    CK --> DL
    REC --> DL
    DM --> DL
    DL --> VF --> RUN
```

Sources: [manifest.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/manifest.py#L2-L9), [build.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/build.py#L1-L12)

## Inside the Phase 0 Asset Manifest

The manifest is called the **provenance root** because it is the first record created and everything downstream can be traced back to it. For each downloaded H5AD, Phase 0 records the original filename, the GEO accession, the exact source URL, the download timestamp, the byte size, and the SHA-256 digest — and it notes explicitly that no FASTQ reprocessing was performed ("the public H5ADs opened and read, so nothing was reprocessed").

Sources: [manifest.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/manifest.py#L22-L45)

One check here is easy to overlook but important to understand. The manifest also compares the file size against the size the server *advertised*:

| Field | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- |
| `bytes` | Actual size on disk |
| `bytes_advertised_by_server` | Size the server reported |
| `size_matches_server` | `true` only when both agree |
| `download_method` | "eight ranged HTTPS workers, reassembled in order" |
| `downloaded_at` | UTC timestamp of the file on disk |

The build exits with a failure code if any size mismatch is detected, so an incomplete download cannot silently advance to the processing stages.

Sources: [manifest.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/manifest.py#L14-L18), [manifest.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/manifest.py#L46-L52)

> [!TIP]
> A ranged parallel download that loses a chunk produces a file that *opens and reads normally* but is simply wrong in the middle. That is precisely why the code cross-checks disk size against server-advertised size in addition to computing the SHA-256 — two independent failure detectors for one failure mode.

## Verifying Your Downloaded Snapshot

Once the release is on disk, a single command verifies every released byte against `DATA_MANIFEST.json`:

```bash
python3 tools/verify_processed_data.py --root .
```

The verifier is strict by design. It walks every entry in the manifest and applies five checks; any failure is printed and the process exits non-zero:

| Check | What it catches |
| :--- | :--- |
| Manifest schema must be `VCDESIGN_PROCESSED_DATA_V1` | Wrong or tampered manifest version |
| Paths must be relative, no `..`, no duplicates | Path traversal / duplicate entries |
| File must exist and **not be a symlink** | Missing files, symlink substitution |
| Byte size must match the manifest | Truncated or padded downloads |
| Streaming SHA-256 must match the manifest | Any content change, even one byte |

Sources: [tools/verify_processed_data.py](tools/verify_processed_data.py#L21-L46), [tools/verify_processed_data.py](tools/verify_processed_data.py#L8-L14)

The frozen reference checkpoint `checkpoints/final_clean_epoch_008.pt` has its SHA-256 (`58da13d2…9484`) recorded in **two independent places** — the run configuration and the processed-data manifest — so a mismatch at either layer exposes a substituted or corrupted checkpoint before it can affect a training run.

Sources: [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md#L28-L31), [configs/paper_run_v1.json](configs/paper_run_v1.json#L41-L43)

## How Provenance Stays Honest During Processing

Verification does not stop at the raw bytes. The four-context processing pipeline follows two design principles worth internalizing. First, the measurement contract (normalization, batch splitting, eligibility gates) was **frozen before any new-context number existed**, and Phase 2 applies it unchanged — "the anchor's recipe applied to a different dataset, not a recipe chosen for that dataset." Second, the dataset audit document is *regenerated from the JSON artifacts on disk rather than transcribed*, so every number in the audit cannot drift from the run that produced it.

Sources: [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L15-L21), [build.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/build.py#L1-L12), [dataset_doc.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/dataset_doc.py#L2-L5)

The audit document then renders the provenance table (accession, bytes, server-size match, SHA-256 prefix, download time per file) and an independent verification section in which every context must pass under a frozen verifier contract — with a deliberately corrupted "witness" asset included, so that *a run whose witness does not fail is itself a failure*. This chain — asset manifest → deterministic build → regenerated audit → independent verification — is what makes the claim "these results came from those bytes" auditable end to end.

Sources: [dataset_doc.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/dataset_doc.py#L18-L33), [dataset_doc.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/dataset_doc.py#L49-L60)

## Where to Go Next

You now know where the data comes from and how its integrity is enforced. For the commands that put this into practice, return to [Reproducing Paper Results](4-reproducing-paper-results). To understand what the frozen `inputs/` assets actually contain and how the four-context measurement contract is defined, continue to [Four-Context Data Contracts](17-four-context-data-contracts). For a deeper treatment of the manifest and hash-verification machinery itself, see [Artifact Verification and SHA-256 Manifests](23-artifact-verification-and-sha-256-manifests), and for the broader system context, [Architecture Overview](6-architecture-overview).


# Architecture Overview



VCDesign-CED is organized around a single architectural conviction: **every scientifically meaningful number is frozen in code before it is computed**. The repository implements finite-budget intervention design for virtual cells — ranking feasible CRISPRi interventions for a source-to-target transition and grading only the executable top-B prefix against independently measured held-out outcomes ([README.md](README.md#L32), [README.md](README.md#L42-L59)). Rather than a research-code sprawl, this is a *contract-driven pipeline*: 18 versioned packages under `src/gene_open_inverse/`, each owning one stage, each carrying a `contract.py` that pre-registers its hypothesis, its legality rules, and every constant that could otherwise be tuned after seeing results. This page maps the whole system; the per-stage mechanics live in the Deep Dive pages that follow.

![VCDesign framework overview](https://github.com/Boom5426/VCDesign-CED/blob/main/assets/vcdesign_overview.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L32-L38), [PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md#L1-L17)

## Architectural Philosophy: Frozen Contracts

The load-bearing pattern in this codebase is the `contract.py` file, present in every stage package. A contract is not configuration; it is a **pre-registration artifact**. The CED contract opens with the directive "Frozen before the first number," states the scientific hypothesis (distillation removes the burden of learning *how to compare* candidates so the ranker only learns *what a candidate does*), and then enumerates what each evaluation phase may legally read ([contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L1-L19)). Three information tiers govern every module: **G_fit** identities may be read for training, **G_select** candidates' measured responses may be used only for grading and never as inputs, and **G_check** is sealed entirely ([contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L16-L19)). Constants — basis rank, ridge folds, penalty grids, seeds — are declared inline with their justification, e.g. `BASIS_RANK = 256  # one value, fixed in advance, no grid` ([contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L50-L55)). Even the scoring rule is contractual: a candidate with no static knowledge modality receives the exactly-neutral score `ALL_MISSING_SCORE = 0.0`, described as "a cosine's own indifference point, fixed here and not tuned" ([contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L30-L36), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L71-L72)).

The same discipline extends system-wide. The four-context data contract is frozen "before any HepG2 or Jurkat number exists," pre-registers three scientific questions, and forbids changing any pre-registered number after seeing a held-context result ([contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L1-L13), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L45-L50)). The evaluation contract carries an explicit freeze date `FROZEN = "2026-09-18"` and even lists metrics retired from the paper, so a reader can audit what was de-scoped ([contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L4-L13)).

Sources: [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L1-L77), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L1-L50), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L1-L32)

## Layered System Architecture

The packages compose into six layers with strictly downward dependencies: data contracts feed a frozen base model, whose outputs feed distillation, whose scores feed the evaluation contract, with baselines and analyses attached at the same evaluation interface, and an integrity layer enforcing the freeze across all of it.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph L1["1 · Data Contracts"]
        FC["four_context_v1<br/>K562 · RPE1 · HepG2 · Jurkat"]
        EC["external_context_v1"]
        DS["freeze manifests<br/>+ response caches"]
    end
    subgraph L2["2 · Frozen Model Layer"]
        MDL["model/* components<br/>knowledge features · dual encoder"]
        FCM["final_clean_model_v1<br/>CLEAN_BASE scorer"]
    end
    subgraph L3["3 · Distillation Layer (CED)"]
        B["basis.py — rank-256 response basis"]
        P["predictor.py — ridge on STRING+MAPKG"]
        F["fuse.py — score fusion"]
        RV["revision_v1 — grouped ridge penalty"]
    end
    subgraph L4["4 · Decision & Evaluation Layer"]
        EV["evaluation_contract_v1<br/>BU@B · MU@B · PHR@B"]
        DC["decision_consistent_effect_v1"]
        UT["action_conditioned_utility_v1<br/>utility_gt_v2"]
    end
    subgraph L5["5 · Baselines & Analyses"]
        EB["external_baselines_v1<br/>GEARS · CellNavi · PHR"]
        OV["open_vocab_generalization_v1<br/>response masking"]
    end
    subgraph L6["6 · Integrity Layer"]
        LK["final_clean_model_v1.lock"]
        CFG["configs/paper_run_v1.json"]
        TV["tools/verify_processed_data.py"]
    end
    DS --> FC
    FC --> FCM
    MDL --> FCM
    FCM --> B
    RV --> P
    B --> F
    P --> F
    F --> EV
    FCM --> EV
    EV --> DC
    EB --> EV
    OV --> EV
    EV --> UT
    LK -. enforces freeze .-> FCM
    LK -. enforces freeze .-> F
    CFG --> LK
    TV -. verifies .-> DS
```

Sources: [PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md#L3-L17), [lock.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/lock.py#L20-L27)

The boundary between Layer 2 and Layer 3 is the paper's central claim made structural. When candidate responses have been measured in other contexts, **direct retrieval** from the base scorer is the recommended route; when they have not, **VCDesign-CED predicted-effect scoring** takes over — but both routes expose the identical downstream interface (candidate pool, budget, outcome-based evaluation), which is why baseline modules can attach at a single point ([README.md](README.md#L61-L68)). The base scorer is deliberately context-agnostic in cross-context experiments: it is "never retrained, never adapted and never told which context it is looking at," an asymmetry the four-context contract declares rather than corrects ([contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L34-L43)).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L61-L68), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L34-L43)

## Module Inventory

Each `_v1`/`_v2` suffix encodes that the package's contract is versioned and frozen; `model/` is the exception — a library of frozen components rather than a pipeline stage.

| Package | Role in the pipeline | Representative surface |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `four_context_v1` | K562/RPE1/HepG2/Jurkat data contracts, build, audits, LOCO folds | `build`, `contexts`, `loco`, `manifest` |
| `final_clean_model_v1` | Final base scorer: training, selection, scoring, pre-evaluation lock | `train`, `select`, `scoring`, `lock` |
| `candidate_effect_distillation_v1` | CED: response basis, ridge effect predictor, fusion, protocol test | `basis`, `predictor`, `fuse`, `run`, `test_protocol` |
| `revision_v1` | Gene-grouped ridge penalty selection (the corrected default) | `grouped_fit`, `test_grouped_fit` |
| `evaluation_contract_v1` | Frozen metric families, budgets, bootstrap statistics, adoption gates | `metrics`, `adoption`, `contract` |
| `decision_consistent_effect_v1` | Decision-consistent effect arms and statistics | `arms`, `stats` |
| `action_conditioned_utility_v1` / `utility_gt_v2` | Utility ground truth: mechanism, stratification, steelman validation | `mechanism`, `steelman`, `validate` |
| `external_baselines_v1` | GEARS, CellNavi, PHR comparator adapters and reporting tables | `gears_fit`, `cellnavi_fit`, `phr`, `tables` |
| `open_vocab_generalization_v1` | Response masking, pool-size, mixture and support analyses | `masking`, `poolsize`, `verify_masking` |
| `external_context_v1` | External corpora: joint build, transfer, zero-shot | `build`, `transfer`, `zeroshot` |
| `measurement_v2_quad` / `rwed_v1` / `evidence_v1` / `ppm_v1` | Quad splitting, RWED estimator, evidence runs, PPM model+decide | `split`, `estimator`, `run` |
| `model/` | Frozen components: knowledge features, dual encoder, decision alignment, GOKA attribution | 10 versioned sub-packages |

Sources: [PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md#L3-L17), [get_repo_structure](src/gene_open_inverse)

## The CED Pipeline Dataflow

Candidate Effect Distillation is the mechanism that transfers ranking ability to candidates whose responses were never measured. The verified dataflow, exactly as exercised in the synthetic demo, is a five-step chain: (1) historical measured responses from G_fit are decomposed by a randomized SVD into a **rank-256 response basis**; (2) G_fit targets are **projected** into that basis; (3) a ridge path fitted on presence-aware STRING+MAPKG static features **predicts basis coordinates** for deployment candidates; (4) predictions are **reconstructed** back into 8248-gene space and zeroed for all-missing candidates; (5) the predicted effect is scored by **cosine against the goal direction** and fused with the base score via per-row z-standardization ([ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L29-L43)).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R["G_fit measured<br/>responses"] -->|"randomized SVD<br/>rank 256"| RB["response basis"]
    RB -->|"project"| PJ["basis-space<br/>targets"]
    K["STRING + MAPKG<br/>static features"] -->|"presence-aware"| RP["RidgePath<br/>5-fold CV"]
    PJ --> RP
    RP -->|"reconstruct"| PE["predicted effect<br/>8248-d gene space"]
    PE -->|"all-missing → 0.0"| CS["cosine vs goal d_q"]
    CS --> FZ["row_z fusion:<br/>z(base) + z(effect)"]
    BS["CLEAN_BASE<br/>base score"] --> FZ
    FZ --> TB["top-B prefix<br/>ranking"]
```

Sources: [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L29-L43), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L50-L72)

Two contract decisions inside this chain deserve architectural attention because they encode scientific intent, not just defaults. The ridge penalty is selected by `held_out_mean_cosine_in_gene_space` rather than squared error, "because the deployment use is a direction comparison and squared error would spend the penalty on magnitude" ([contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L62-L68)). And the pipeline's most consequential legality rule is stated as a constant with a name: `PREDICTED_EFFECT_IS_NOT_AN_INFERENCE_INPUT` — the predicted effect is a function of static knowledge alone, so no measured response of the scored candidate ever leaks into its own score ([contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L73-L76)).

> [!TIP]
> The demo imports `row_z` from `final_clean_model_v1.scoring` ([ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L7-L8)) — evidence that fusion normalization is a shared primitive owned by the base-scorer package, not re-implemented per stage. One primitive, one definition, everywhere.

Sources: [ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L7-L8), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/candidate_effect_distillation_v1/contract.py#L62-L76)

## The Evaluation Contract

Evaluation is itself a frozen module, not an ad-hoc notebook. The contract pins the budget family `(10, 20, 50)` with `BU@20` as primary, assigns roles across five metric families (BU primary, MU secondary, HvHit experimental efficiency, PHR validity guardrail, QWR consistency), and fixes the inferential machinery: median of paired per-row differences, 10,000 bootstrap replicates, clustering by query gene ([contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L7-L20)).
