Critically, the contract also encodes the **decision rule** — the K562 locked `G_check` serves as a sealed anchor, three held-out contexts (RPE1, HepG2, Jurkat) run under the `MASKED` decision regime, and adoption is gated by `MIN_WORTHWHILE_GAIN = 0.005`, a context-majority of 2, and a QWR gate of 0.5, yielding explicit `ADOPT_NEW_METHOD` / `KEEP_INCUMBENT` verdicts ([contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L21-L32)).

| Contract element | Frozen value | Function |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Budgets | `(10, 20, 50)`; primary 20 | Finite-budget prefixes actually executed |
| Metric families | BU, MU, HvHit, PHR, QWR | Primary / secondary / efficiency / guardrail / consistency roles |
| Statistic | Median paired difference + mean beside it | Robust within-query comparison |
| Bootstrap | 10,000 replicates, seed `20260916`, cluster = query gene | Pre-registered uncertainty |
| Decision regime | `MASKED` on RPE1, HepG2, Jurkat; K562 `G_check` sealed | Response masking at decision time |
| Adoption gates | `gain ≥ 0.005`, 2-of-3 contexts, QWR ≥ 0.5 | Mechanical accept/reject, no judgment call |

Sources: [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L7-L32)

## Integrity Architecture: Locks, Manifests, and Verification

The freeze is enforced by machinery, not by convention. **Phase F (`lock.py`)** runs *before* `G_check` is touched: it hashes every source file of the four packages the locked evaluation depends on (a combined SHA-256 over per-file digests, chosen because "a commit hash alone does not identify the code that produced this lock" in an authoring checkout with uncommitted work), records the git commit and platform, hashes checkpoints, and **refuses to overwrite an existing lock record** — so a second, adjusted run cannot quietly replace the first ([lock.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/lock.py#L1-L9), [lock.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/lock.py#L30-L60)). The evaluation module then reads its checkpoints and predictor penalty *from this record* rather than from any tunable source. Downstream, `configs/paper_run_v1.json` pins every asset path and carries `selected_checkpoint_sha256` for the frozen `FINAL_CLEAN_EPOCH_008` checkpoint selected by rule ([paper_run_v1.json](configs/paper_run_v1.json#L17-L43)). `tools/verify_processed_data.py` closes the loop by verifying processed data against SHA-256 manifests, and `evidence_v1` provides the run-evidence layer ([PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md#L13-L16)).

> [!TIP]
> The lock's file-hashing strategy reveals a subtle design trade-off: because the authoring checkout had uncommitted work, identity was established by *content* (SHA-256 of every `.py` in `CODE_PACKAGES`) rather than by *history* (git HEAD). This means the published results are reproducible from file bytes alone — which is precisely what `tools/verify_processed_data.py` audits downstream.

Sources: [lock.py](src/gene_open_inverse/final_clean_model_v1/lock.py#L1-L60), [paper_run_v1.json](configs/paper_run_v1.json#L17-L43), [PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md#L13-L16)

## Entry Points and Execution Model

Execution is uniformly module-level — no driver script orchestrates the pipeline. Each stage is invoked as `python3 -m gene_open_inverse.<package>.<entry>`, which keeps stages independently runnable and auditable in isolation. The six canonical entry points ([PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md#L19-L28)):

| Task | Entry point |
| :--- | :--- |
| Synthetic end-to-end check | `python3 examples/ced_demo.py` |
| Protocol tests | `python3 -m pytest -q` |
| Train the final base scorer | `python3 -m gene_open_inverse.final_clean_model_v1.train` |
| Candidate Effect Distillation | `python3 -m gene_open_inverse.candidate_effect_distillation_v1.run` |
| Four-context processing | `python3 -m gene_open_inverse.four_context_v1.build` |
| External-baseline reports | `python3 -m gene_open_inverse.external_baselines_v1.tables` |

Sources: [PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md#L19-L31)

Note the architectural role of `pytest -q`: protocol modules such as `candidate_effect_distillation_v1.test_protocol`, `external_baselines_v1.test_protocol`, and `open_vocab_generalization_v1.test_protocol` are executable contracts — after the post-review corrections, these checks now **fail the test suite** when their legality invariants do not hold, rather than only reporting failure in standalone runners ([README.md](README.md#L125-L134)). The full command sequence for reproducing paper numbers lives in REPRODUCE.md, which is the operational counterpart to this page ([PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md#L30-L31)).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L125-L134), [PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md](PROJECT_STRUCTURE.md#L30-L31)

# Problem Formulation: Finite-Budget Ranking



This page defines the formal problem that every module in `gene_open_inverse` exists to solve: cellular intervention design as **finite-budget ranking over a variable candidate set**. A solver ranks feasible interventions for a requested source-to-target transition, and evaluation scores only the executable top-$B$ prefix using independently measured held-out outcomes. The formulation is deliberately decision-shaped rather than prediction-shaped — the deliverable is an ordered shortlist, not a forecast — and everything downstream (metrics, protocols, distillation) inherits its constraints from the definitions on this page.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L40-L46)

## From First Principles: What Makes This a Ranking Problem

The design task starts from a question an experimentalist can actually afford to answer: *given a desired cellular transition, which perturbations should we run next, and only the next $B$ of them?* Three properties distinguish this from a standard regression or classification setup. First, the output is an **ordering** — the solver must arrange candidates by expected usefulness, because the experiment consumes a prefix of the list, not a point estimate. Second, the candidate set is **variable**: the legal pool's size and membership change with the cellular context and the candidate stratum being scored, so the formulation never fixes a vocabulary at training time. Third, the score of a decision is computed from **independently measured held-out outcomes**, never from the model's own predictions — the ranking is graded against reality, not against itself.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L40-L46), [four_context_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L87-L97)

This decision-shaped framing shows up directly in the metric machinery: the contract computes exact coefficients for how much a two-element swap in the ranking changes the primary aggregate, and explicitly assigns **zero decision value to pairs that sit entirely outside every actionable budget** — a candidate ranked 60th when the budget ends at 50 is not part of the problem.

Sources: [decision_alignment_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L156-L176)

## The Entities: Query, Candidate Pool, Budget

The formulation fixes three objects that all evaluation code treats as first-class.

**Query.** A query is a perturbed identity $q$ with a measured source-to-target transition. Not every measured identity is a valid query: Phase 1 of the utility contract first decides whether the transition is *measurable at all*, using a shared latent transition energy $E_q = \langle d_A^q, d_B^q\rangle$ tested against a mismatched-partner permutation null with Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control at 0.05 plus a positivity requirement. The design rationale is stated plainly in the code: "A query is only a question if its transition is measurable at all."

Sources: [utility_gt_v2/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/utility_gt_v2/contract.py#L17-L28), [utility_gt_v2/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/utility_gt_v2/contract.py#L8-L16)

**Candidate pool.** The candidate axis is context-defined and role-blind: "every usable identity in the context, whatever its training role." Crucially, queries are a subset of candidates, and the production candidate vocabulary stays *complete* — a diagnostic module exists solely to confirm that restricting the pool to eligible identities would change conclusions, and it explicitly notes that "the production candidate vocabulary stays complete; nothing here filters candidates by response reliability."

Sources: [four_context_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L84-L86), [utility_gt_v2/pool_composition.py](src/gene_open_inverse/utility_gt_v2/pool_composition.py#L1-L11)

**Budget.** The deployment budgets are frozen at $B \in \{10, 20, 50\}$ with $B = 20$ as the primary, fixed before any model comparison. A query's legal pool must be larger than the largest budget, or the evaluation stops rather than reports.

Sources: [evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L7-L9), [decision_alignment_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L19-L23)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph ELIG["Phase 1: Query Eligibility"]
        A["Two disjoint measurement views<br/>d_A, d_B"] --> B["E_q = <d_A^q, d_B^q>"]
        B --> C["Permutation null vs<br/>mismatched partners"]
        C --> D{"BH-FDR ≤ 0.05<br/>AND E_q > 0?"}
        D -->|yes| E["Eligible query"]
        D -->|no| F["Not a question"]
    end
    E --> G["Query axis (rectangular)"]
    subgraph POOL["Candidate Pool (complete, role-blind)"]
        H["Every usable identity<br/>in the context"]
    end
    G --> I["Solver ranks pool by score s_qc"]
    H --> I
    I --> J["Top-B prefix<br/>B ∈ {10, 20, 50}"]
    J --> K["Graded by held-out<br/>independent view"]
```

Because queries are a strict subset of candidates, the score and utility matrices are **rectangular** ($[\text{queries}] \times [\text{candidates in stratum}]$): the query axis stays fixed while the pool it ranks shrinks. This is what separates candidate generalization from context generalization — two questions the protocol refuses to collapse into one number.

Sources: [four_context_v1/evaluate.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L1-L17), [four_context_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L103-L107)

## The Ground-Truth Utility: Distance Reduction Without a Denominator

The quantity a ranking is ultimately graded against is the **reduction in squared endpoint distance** a candidate buys for a query:

$$V_{qc} = \|d^*_q\|^2 - \|r^*_c - d^*_q\|^2 = 2\langle r^*_c, d^*_q\rangle - \|r^*_c\|^2$$

where $d^*_q$ is the query's latent desired direction and $r^*_c$ the candidate's latent response. The implementation realizes this as a four-way cross-view estimate: with $M = \text{first} \cdot \text{second}^\top$, the value is $M[c,q] + M[q,c] - M[c,c]$ — "no division, no clipping, no per-query rescaling."

Sources: [utility_gt_v2/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/utility_gt_v2/contract.py#L29-L45), [utility_gt_v2/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/utility_gt_v2/contract.py#L135-L150)

The missing denominator is a deliberate architectural decision with a documented failure history. An earlier formulation divided by an estimate of $\|d^*_q\|^2$; since that is a per-query constant it never changed a within-query ranking, but whenever the estimate came out non-positive it **flipped the sign of every utility in the row** and produced a catastrophic metric tail. Dropping it "removes that failure mode by construction rather than by filtering" — the ranking metric family is invariant to positive per-query affine rescaling, so the removal is exactly neutral for the decision layer.

Sources: [utility_gt_v2/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/utility_gt_v2/contract.py#L31-L43)

> [!TIP]
> The contract also exposes `physical_bound_violation`, which flags $V_{qc} > E_q$ — algebraically an impossible negative squared distance. The code's comment is precise about interpretation: this reads out **estimator variance**, not a candidate "overshooting" the goal, so it is a measurement-quality diagnostic, not a candidate filter.

Sources: [utility_gt_v2/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/utility_gt_v2/contract.py#L182-L192)

## Why the Estimates Are Unbiased: The Two-View Measurement Discipline

Every quantity in the formulation is built from **two independent measurement views**, so no term is ever a self inner product of one noisy vector — this is what makes the estimators unbiased for the latent quantity rather than inflated by measurement variance. The query-side energy $E_q$ is unbiased for $\|d^*_q\|^2$ precisely because the two views are measured on disjoint batches, so the noise cross-term vanishes in expectation. Phase 2 then exploits the same structure for the decision itself: it asks whether a budget prefix ranked by one measurement view keeps its experimental utility when graded under the *independent* view, in both directions ("first ranks, second grades" and vice versa) — and the runner states its scope explicitly: "Nothing here trains, and nothing here reads a model score."

Sources: [utility_gt_v2/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/utility_gt_v2/contract.py#L8-L16), [utility_gt_v2/run.py](src/gene_open_inverse/utility_gt_v2/run.py#L1-L13), [utility_gt_v2/run.py](src/gene_open_inverse/utility_gt_v2/run.py#L18-L22)

This cross-view grading discipline is the foundation of the held-out evaluation protocol (covered in detail in [Held-Out Context Evaluation Protocol](9-held-out-context-evaluation-protocol)), but it is worth noting here that it is inherited, not reinvented: the four-context contract reuses the frozen A/B batch hash, quarter refinement, minimum cell threshold, and the `QUERY_ELIGIBILITY_V1` gate from the K562 lock, applying them unchanged to each new context.

Sources: [four_context_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L25-L48)

## Legality of an Ordering: Self-Exclusion and Frozen Tie-Breaking

Ranking is only well-defined once the ordering rule is frozen, and the formulation delegates this to a single primitive, `stable_order`: **descending score, ties broken by ascending candidate-ID string, the query's own entry masked to $-\infty$ and then removed**, with an optional static coverage mask for open-vocabulary settings. The contract's rationale is blunt about why the tie rule matters: "a method that emits a constant score gets a deterministic ordering and not a favorable one." Every downstream metric — from the primary BU@B to the high-value count — calls this same primitive rather than re-implementing sort logic.

Sources: [open_vocab_dual_encoder_v1/metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/open_vocab_dual_encoder_v1/metrics.py#L18-L28), [decision_alignment_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L1-L11)

Self-exclusion also has to survive pool restriction, and the four-context evaluator documents a real hazard: when a query is *not* in the stratum's pool, the excluded index must be `None` rather than `-1`, because `stable_order` would read `-1` as the last candidate "and silently delete a real one." The excluded index semantics are therefore part of the formulation's interface contract, not an implementation detail.

Sources: [four_context_v1/evaluate.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L8-L17), [evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py#L17-L33)

## Grading the Prefix: Outcome-Based References (Sketch)

The primary statistic of the formulation — detailed fully in [Ranking Metrics: BU@B, MU@B, PHR@B](8-ranking-metrics-buatb-muatb-phratb) — normalizes each query's discounted utility at the chosen budget against two references computed from the *measured utility row itself*: a random reference (the plain mean over the legal pool; under a uniform permutation the discount cancels, so no Monte Carlo is needed) and an oracle reference (the utility row ranking the pool). The normalized score is **not clipped** — worse than random is negative — and a degenerate-denominator identifiability gate halts comparison rather than reporting ratios with no scale.

Sources: [decision_alignment_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L101-L118), [decision_alignment_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L157-L165), [decision_alignment_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L199-L215)

| Object | Definition | Role in the formulation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Legal pool | All candidates in the stratum, minus the query itself | The ranked universe per query |
| Random reference | Mean utility over the legal pool | Zero-skill baseline; discount cancels |
| Oracle reference | Discounted utility of the utility-true ordering | Ceiling for normalization |
| Denominator floor | $10^{-8}$ absolute | Guards degenerate normalizations; observed minima were 0.038 and 4.15 |
| Identifiability gate | ≤ 1% of queries may have degenerate denominators | Stops the comparison instead of fabricating scale |

Sources: [decision_alignment_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L16-L23), [utility_gt_v2/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/utility_gt_v2/contract.py#L40-L43)

## One Decision Interface, Two Information Regimes

The formulation's most consequential property is that the downstream decision interface — *candidate pool, experimental budget, outcome-based evaluation* — is identical regardless of what information the solver holds about candidates. Two regimes share it:

| Property | Direct response retrieval | VCDesign-CED predicted-effect scoring |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Candidate information at decision time | Measured candidate responses available | Candidate responses unavailable (masked / unmeasured) |
| Solver output | Same ranked pool interface | Same ranked pool interface |
| Evaluation | Same outcome-based grading | Same outcome-based grading |
| Hard constraint | — | Deployment candidate's measured response is never an input |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L50-L59)

The "never an input" constraint is enforced structurally, not by convention: it appears in the four-context qualification checklist as `no_candidate_response_in_inference_features`, and candidates missing all supported knowledge modalities receive a frozen all-missing score defined by the protocol rather than an ad-hoc fallback.

Sources: [four_context_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L87-L97), [README.md](README.md#L92-L104)

## What Varies, What Is Frozen

The formulation draws a sharp boundary between the parts of the problem that vary per evaluation and the parts that are fixed before any result exists.

| Frozen (before any model result) | Varies per evaluation |
| :--- | :--- |
| Budgets $\{10, 20, 50\}$, primary $B=20$ | The candidate pool (context and stratum) |
| Stable ordering rule and self-exclusion semantics | Which queries are eligible (context's query rule) |
| High-value quantile (0.95), bootstrap seed (20260916), replicate count (10000) | The measurement views consumed for ranking vs grading |
| Alignment contract SHA-256 (runs stop on hash mismatch) | Stratum selection: `ALL`, `SEEN_CANDIDATE`, `UNSEEN_CANDIDATE`, `COMMON4` |

Sources: [evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L7-L18), [four_context_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L103-L107), [decision_alignment_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L29-L34)

One consequence deserves emphasis: restricting the pool to a stratum **moves the per-query random and oracle references**, because within a stratum "the achievable ceiling is the stratum's own ceiling." Absolute numbers from one stratum are therefore not comparable to another's — only paired differences between methods inside one stratum are. This is why cross-stratum comparisons in later pages are always paired.

Sources: [four_context_v1/evaluate.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L4-L8)

> [!TIP]
> The evaluation contract hard-codes its adoption semantics alongside the metric definitions — `MIN_WORTHWHILE_GAIN = 0.005`, `CONTEXT_MAJORITY = 2`, and `QWR_GATE = 0.5` sit in the same file as the budget list. Reading that one module gives you the complete decision-theoretic envelope of the benchmark: what is measured, at what scale a difference counts, and how many contexts must agree before `ADOPT_NEW_METHOD` beats `KEEP_INCUMBENT`.

Sources: [evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L24-L32)

## How the Pieces Connect

The module graph below shows how the formulation decomposes into code: the utility contract owns what "good" means, the alignment contract owns how orderings are scored, the four-context contracts own who may be a query and what the pool is, and the evaluation contract owns the frozen decision semantics.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph UTIL["utility_gt_v2"]
        UC["contract.py<br/>V_qc, eligibility E_q, BH-FDR"]
        UR["run.py<br/>Phase 1 + Phase 2<br/>no training, no model scores"]
    end
    subgraph ALIGN["model/decision_alignment_v1"]
        AC["contract.py<br/>RU@B, nRU@B, references,<br/>identifiability gate, SHA-256"]
    end
    subgraph ORDER["model/open_vocab_dual_encoder_v1"]
        SO["metrics.py<br/>stable_order primitive"]
    end
    subgraph FC["four_context_v1"]
        FCC["contract.py<br/>query/candidate rules,<br/>strata, qualification"]
        FCE["evaluate.py<br/>rectangular stratum metrics,<br/>fusion, paired stats"]
    end
    subgraph EC["evaluation_contract_v1"]
        ECC["contract.py<br/>budgets, primary metric,<br/>adoption gates"]
        ECM["metrics.py<br/>BU/MU/HvHit/PHR/QWR rows"]
    end
    UC --> AC
    AC --> SO
    SO --> FCE
    SO --> ECM
    FCC --> FCE
    AC --> FCE
    EC --> ECM
```

Sources: [utility_gt_v2/run.py](src/gene_open_inverse/utility_gt_v2/run.py#L1-L13), [four_context_v1/evaluate.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L36-L84), [evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py#L1-L16)

For a minimal executable sketch of the decision half of this interface — features to predicted effect to goal alignment to a fused ranked prefix — the synthetic demo in `examples/ced_demo.py` exercises the full path on random data and prints the top-5 prefix, making it the fastest way to see the formulation as live code.

Sources: [examples/ced_demo.py](examples/ced_demo.py#L1-L49)

## Where the Formulation Leads

Everything downstream of this page refines one of its four objects. The scoring layer is formalized in [Ranking Metrics: BU@B, MU@B, PHR@B](8-ranking-metrics-buatb-muatb-phratb); the measurement-side discipline that makes grading trustworthy continues in [Held-Out Context Evaluation Protocol](9-held-out-context-evaluation-protocol); the two information regimes are compared empirically in [Decision Routes: Retrieval versus Prediction](10-decision-routes-retrieval-versus-prediction); and the context-level rules for who queries what are unpacked in [Four-Context Data Contracts](17-four-context-data-contracts). The leakage implications of the query/candidate role split — why the anchor context is queried on `G_select` identities only — are treated in [Leakage Prevention and Identity-Level Cross-Validation](21-leakage-prevention-and-identity-level-cross-validation).


# Ranking Metrics: BU@B, MU@B, PHR@B



This page explains the ranking metrics that grade every candidate-ranking decision in VCDesign: **BU@B** (Budgeted Utility), **MU@B** (Mean Utility), **HvHit@B** (High-Value Hit count), and **PHR@B** (Perturbation Hit Rate), plus the paired **QWR** (Quadrant Win Rate) forms derived from BU vectors. All four families are computed per evaluation row by a single function, `row_metrics`, under a frozen evaluation contract that fixes the budgets, the tie-breaking rule, and the statistic used to pool them. The implementations live in `evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py`, and every primitive they rely on — the ordering rule and the normalization — is imported from frozen modules under `src/gene_open_inverse/model/` rather than re-implemented locally.

This page sits in the *Evaluation Framework* cluster: it assumes you know what a candidate pool and a finite budget are from [Problem Formulation: Finite-Budget Ranking](7-problem-formulation-finite-budget-ranking), and it precedes the protocol-level details in [Held-Out Context Evaluation Protocol](9-held-out-context-evaluation-protocol).

## The Frozen Metric Family

The evaluation contract V1 declares the metric families, their roles, and the deployment budgets as module-level constants, so no run can silently change what is being measured. Budgets are frozen at `B = (10, 20, 50)` with **BU@20 as the primary metric**; the family tuple is `("BU", "MU", "HvHit", "PHR", "QWR")`, where QWR is a derived consistency metric rather than an independently computed ranking score. Three older metrics — `MBRU`, `Best@B`, and `J RU@B` — are explicitly retired from the paper, which is why BU@20 rather than a multi-budget aggregate anchors the headline results.

Sources: [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L7-L14)

Each family carries a distinct decision role declared in the contract: BU is the **primary** ranking-quality signal, MU is the **secondary** check that guards against discounted-gain artifacts, HvHit measures **experimental efficiency** (how often picks land in the top-utility tail), PHR is the **validity guardrail** (whether picks have any realized, independently graded benefit), and QWR measures **consistency** between paired methods. The pooling statistic is also frozen here: the *median of paired per-row differences, mean reported beside it*, estimated by 10,000-replicate bootstrap with seed `20260916`, clustered by query gene.

| Family | Role in contract | Per-row definition | Requires |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| BU@B | Primary | Normalized discounted Ranked Utility (`nRU@B`) | scores, utility |
| MU@B | Secondary | Plain mean of the utilities of the top-B picks | scores, utility |
| HvHit@B | Experimental efficiency | Count of picks ≥ 95th percentile of the legal pool | scores, utility |
| PHR@B | Validity guardrail | Fraction of picks with realized `J > 0` | scores, utility, **realized J** |
| QWR | Consistency | Win rate of one method's BU vector against another | two BU vectors |

Sources: [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L10-L12), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L16-L19)

The `row_metrics` docstring records a deliberate design decision: BU@B is defined as the frozen `nRU@B`, MU@B as the frozen `Mean@B`, and HvHit@B as the frozen `HighValueCount@B`, and the test suite **asserts these identities against the existing evaluator rather than assuming them**. This means the contract-page naming and the per-row computation cannot drift apart without a test failing.

Sources: [metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py#L1-L7)

## How One Row Is Ranked: Self-Exclusion and the Stable Tie Order

Every row is one query in one view, ranked over the **self-excluded legal pool** of one candidate stratum in a frozen stable tie order (`metrics.py`, module docstring). Concretely, `row_metrics` takes four aligned arrays — `scores`, `utility`, `candidate_ids`, and `self_positions` — where `self_positions[i]` is where row `i`'s query identity sits in the stratum, or `-1` if it is absent. When the position is non-negative, the ranking order is produced with that index excluded, and then the excluded slot is removed from the order array so the picked prefix contains only legal candidates.

Sources: [metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py#L17-L23), [metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py#L34-L39)

The ordering primitive itself, `stable_order`, is borrowed from the dual-encoder model package and never re-implemented per metric. It sets the excluded (and any masked) candidate scores to `-inf`, then applies `np.lexsort((candidate_ids_as_strings, -rank))`: **descending by score, ties broken by ascending candidate ID**. The tie rule is a correctness guarantee, not a convenience — the alignment contract notes that a method emitting a constant score gets a deterministic ordering and not a favorable one, which closes the loophole where ties could be arranged to flatter a comparator.

Sources: [metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/open_vocab_dual_encoder_v1/metrics.py#L17-L27), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L8-L11)

The module interaction structure is deliberately shallow — one metrics function, two frozen primitive modules, and one optional realized-J producer:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph ec["evaluation_contract_v1"]
        EC["contract.py<br/>BUDGETS · ROLES ·<br/>HIGH_VALUE_QUANTILE"]
        EM["metrics.py<br/>row_metrics · qwr"]
        AD["adoption.py<br/>decide (G1–G7)"]
    end
    subgraph model["model/ (frozen primitives)"]
        OA["open_vocab_dual_encoder_v1/metrics.py<br/>stable_order"]
        DA["decision_alignment_v1/contract.py<br/>discount · RU@B ·<br/>query_references · nRU@B"]
    end
    EB["external_baselines_v1/phr.py<br/>realized J matrices"]
    EM -->|"reads budgets,<br/>quantile"| EC
    EM -->|"orders candidates"| OA
    EM -->|"normalizes BU"| DA
    EB -.->|"realized_j (optional input)"| EM
    EM -.->|"per-row metric vectors"| AD
    AD -->|"gate thresholds"| EC
```

Sources: [metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py#L12-L14), [adoption.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/adoption.py#L7-L13)

## BU@B: Normalized Discounted Ranked Utility

BU@B is a DCG-style discounted gain, normalized so that a query's score is interpretable **relative to two references computed from the frozen ground-truth utility itself**. The discount is `d_r = 1 / log₂(r + 1)` for ranks `r = 1..B`, fixed and never tuned, and `RU@B` is the discount-weighted mean of the utilities placed in predicted rank order: `RU@B = Σ d_r · U_(r) / Z_B`, where `Z_B = Σ d_r`.

Sources: [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L43-L48), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L66-L72)

Normalization is performed by `query_references` and `normalized_ranked_utility`. For each query, the references are computed over the *self-excluded legal pool ordered by true utility*: the random reference `RU_rand` and the oracle `RU_oracle@B`, whose difference forms the denominator. The final score is `nRU@B = (RU@B − RU_rand) / (RU_oracle@B − RU_rand)` — so **1.0 means oracle-quality ranking and 0.0 means random**.

Sources: [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L85-L103), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L121-L128)

Two implementation details matter for interpreting published BU numbers. First, the random reference needs **no Monte Carlo sampling**: under a uniform permutation the expected utility is the same at every rank, so the discount weights cancel and the reference is simply the plain mean over the legal pool — a closed-form identity, not an estimate. Second, the normalized score is deliberately **not clipped**: a ranking worse than random returns a negative BU@B, and a degenerate denominator (oracle indistinguishable from random for that query) is floored at `1e-8` and policed by a separate identifiability gate that halts comparison rather than reporting a ratio with no scale.

Sources: [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L86-L91), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L121-L128), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L191-L197)

The whole BU pipeline is under hash-lock: the alignment contract file that defines Ranked Utility, nRU, and MBRU carries a recorded SHA-256, `verify_contract` recomputes it at run time, and **the run stops rather than reporting numbers under a contract that no longer says what it said**.

Sources: [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L1-L7), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/model/decision_alignment_v1/contract.py#L29-L40)

## MU@B and HvHit@B: The Undiscounted Complements

Inside the same per-row budget loop, `row_metrics` slices the utilities of the top-B picks (`picked = utility[row, order[:budget]]`) and computes the two simpler families directly on that prefix. **MU@B is the plain arithmetic mean** of the picked utilities — no discounting, no normalization — which makes it a robust sanity check on BU: a method cannot score well on BU@B while systematically picking mediocre candidates, and the adoption gate explicitly requires that MU@20 is never reversed relative to the incumbent. **HvHit@B is a count**, not a rate: the number of picks whose utility is at least the 95th-percentile threshold of the legal pool, where the threshold is computed with `np.quantile` on the legal utilities after self-exclusion.

Sources: [metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py#L42-L48), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L14)

The three utility-based families answer deliberately different questions, which is why all three appear in the same output dictionary keyed `"<family>@<budget>"`:

| Property | BU@B | MU@B | HvHit@B |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Discounts by rank | Yes (`1/log₂(r+1)`) | No | No |
| Normalized per query | Yes (oracle vs. random) | No | No |
| Scale | Unitless, ~0 (random) to 1 (oracle) | Raw utility units | Integer count |
| Sensitive to | Top-heavy ordering quality | Average pick quality | Tail (top-5%) retrieval |
| Paired statistic | Median of per-row differences | Median of per-row differences | Median of per-row differences |

Sources: [metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py#L31-L48), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L16-L17)

## PHR@B: Realized Validity, Never Approximated

PHR@B asks a question the other three cannot: of the B candidates actually selected, **what fraction had a realized, independently measured benefit** — encoded in a realized matrix `J` where a positive entry means the pick produced a positive graded response gain. `row_metrics` computes it as the mean of the indicator `J[row, order[:budget]] > 0` across the picked prefix, and the function signature enforces honesty about data availability: **PHR is returned only when a realized `J` matrix is supplied; it is never approximated**. When `realized_j` is absent, the output dictionary simply contains no PHR keys, and downstream consumers must treat PHR as unavailable rather than imputed.

Sources: [metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py#L21-L23), [metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py#L49-L50)

The realized `J` matrices for the external contexts are produced by `external_baselines_v1/phr.py` under a strict quarter-gate construction. The four-way data build splits each context into quarters (Q0–Q3) that pair into two disjoint views, and `J` **exists only on the four-way sub-pool** — identities with cell counts above the minimum in all four quarters. For a view-v row, the action is chosen on side v's quarter pair (the same quarters that built the row's query), while `J` is realized on side 1−v's pair, "which nothing else touched" — a proposer/grader split that prevents the selection side from leaking into the grading side.

Sources: [phr.py](src/gene_open_inverse/external_baselines_v1/phr.py#L8-L12), [phr.py](src/gene_open_inverse/external_baselines_v1/phr.py#L63-L84)

Before any PHR number is reported, a reconstruction gate proves the quarter decomposition is faithful: for every four-way identity, the cell-count-weighted mean of Q0 and Q1 must equal view A's response and the weighted mean of Q2 and Q3 must equal view B's, within a frozen tolerance, and the evaluation pack's responses must byte-match the build's side responses (`pack_error == 0.0`). This is why the contract labels PHR a **validity guardrail** — it certifies that selections are backed by real outcomes, and the adoption gate rejects a method whose PHR@20 state is negative.

Sources: [phr.py](src/gene_open_inverse/external_baselines_v1/phr.py#L34-L60), [adoption.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/adoption.py#L21-L22)

## QWR: Two Forms of the Same Win Count

`qwr` is the smallest function in the module and the only one that operates on **pooled vectors rather than raw scores**: given two per-row BU@B vectors (a method and a comparator), it counts wins, losses, and ties per row. It returns two win rates that answer different questions, and the docstring is explicit about which is which: **`paper` = wins over all rows** (the paper-facing form, comparator BASE) and **`gate` = wins over decided rows** (the adoption form, comparator the incumbent). The gate form drops ties from the denominator, so a comparator that ties on most rows cannot inflate the consistency signal; `tie_fraction` is reported alongside so the severity of the tie mass is always visible.

| Attribute | `paper` form | `gate` form |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Numerator | Rows where method > comparator | Same wins |
| Denominator | All rows | Wins + losses only (ties excluded) |
| Comparator | BASE | Incumbent |
| Consumer | Paper tables | Adoption gate `G7` (`QWR_gate20 > 0.5`) |
| Tie handling | Counted in denominator | Removed from denominator, reported as `tie_fraction` |

Sources: [metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py#L54-L68), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L28)

## From Per-Row Vectors to the Adoption Gate

The metric vectors are consumed by `adoption.decide`, a pure function of pooled numbers, through seven checks (G1–G7). The pooled inputs are MASKED paired contrasts — the contract freezes the decision regime as `DECISION_REGIME = "MASKED"` on the primary contexts RPE1, HepG2, and Jurkat — and each check reads a different slice of the metric system: BU@20's sign state and effect size, per-context medians and confidence intervals, the MU@20/HvHit@20/PHR@20 states, and the gate-form QWR. Note how each metric family's contract role maps onto exactly one gate check, which is the practical payoff of declaring `ROLES` as frozen constants.

| Gate | Check | Metric consumed | Threshold |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| G1 | BU@20 state positive | BU@B | `POSITIVE` |
| G2 | BU@20 at least worthwhile | BU@B | median ≥ `0.005` |
| G3 | Context majority positive | BU@B per context | ≥ 2 of 3 contexts |
| G4 | No context wholly negative | BU@B per context | upper CI ≥ 0 everywhere |
| G5 | MU@20 not reversed | MU@B | state ≠ `NEGATIVE` |
| G6 | HvHit@20 and PHR@20 not worse | HvHit@B, PHR@B | states ≠ `NEGATIVE` |
| G7 | QWR gate above half | QWR (gate form) | `> 0.5` |

Sources: [adoption.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/adoption.py#L14-L27), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L22-L28)

The full data flow from a scored pool to an adoption verdict is a single acyclic pass — the concept relationship below is the reference map for this entire page:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph row["One evaluation row: query × candidate stratum"]
        S["scores[row]"]
        U["utility[row]<br/>(frozen GT)"]
        SP["self_positions[row]"]
        IDS["candidate_ids"]
        J["realized_j[row]<br/>(four-way sub-pool only)"]
    end
    subgraph primitives["Frozen primitives"]
        SO["stable_order:<br/>descending score ·<br/>ascending-ID ties ·<br/>self-exclusion"]
        REF["query_references:<br/>RU_rand (legal mean) ·<br/>RU_oracle@B · denominator"]
    end
    subgraph metrics["row_metrics output, B ∈ {10, 20, 50}"]
        BU["BU@B = nRU@B<br/>(unclipped)"]
        MU["MU@B = mean(picked)"]
        HV["HvHit@B = count ≥ Q0.95(legal)"]
        PHR["PHR@B = mean(1[J>0])<br/>only if J supplied"]
    end
    QWR["qwr(): paper & gate forms"]
    GATE["adoption.decide:<br/>G1–G7 → ADOPT / KEEP"]
    S --> SO
    SP --> SO
    IDS --> SO
    SO -->|"order[:B]"| MU
    SO -->|"order[:B]"| HV
    SO -->|"ordered utilities"| BU
    U --> REF
    REF -->|"normalization"| BU
    U --> MU
    U --> HV
    J --> PHR
    SO -->|"picks"| PHR
    BU --> QWR
    QWR --> GATE
    MU --> GATE
    HV --> GATE
    PHR --> GATE
```

Sources: [metrics.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/metrics.py#L17-L51), [adoption.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/adoption.py#L7-L28)

> [!TIP]
> The two identities most worth internalizing when reading published tables: (1) a BU@B of exactly `0.0` means the method ranked no better than random *for that query*, because the random reference is the closed-form legal-pool mean — discount weights cancel under uniform permutation; (2) a missing PHR@B column is **not** an approximation or a zero — the function refuses to emit PHR without a realized `J` matrix, so absence certifies the row is outside the four-way sub-pool.

> [!TIP]
> If you ever see constant scores feeding these metrics, the ordering is still fair: `stable_order` breaks ties by ascending candidate-ID string via `lexsort`, so a degenerate scorer gets a deterministic, identity-based order rather than one that could be arranged to flatter it — this is asserted in the alignment contract, not just documented.

## Where to Go Next

With the metric definitions in hand, the natural reading order is: [Held-Out Context Evaluation Protocol](9-held-out-context-evaluation-protocol) for how rows and pools are constructed before `row_metrics` ever runs, then [Decision Routes: Retrieval versus Prediction](10-decision-routes-retrieval-versus-prediction) for how the two scoring routes produce the `scores` input. If you want to see where BU@20 numbers come from in practice, [Score Fusion and Beta Selection](14-score-fusion-and-beta-selection) covers the CED scoring branch, and the headline pooled contrasts are summarized in [Key Benchmark Findings](26-key-benchmark-findings). For the guarantees that keep these metrics honest across identities, continue to [Leakage Prevention and Identity-Level Cross-Validation](21-leakage-prevention-and-identity-level-cross-validation).


# Held-Out Context Evaluation Protocol



This page specifies how VCDesign grades generalization to a **cell context that contributed no training data**. The protocol is implemented in `src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/`: a leave-one-context-out (LOCO) harness in which one of the four measured cell lines (K562, RPE1, HepG2, Jurkat) is withheld entirely, an effect predictor is fitted only on the other three, and the held context is then graded on a fixed candidate population with a frozen base ranker as the reference arm. The page covers fold construction, per-context train/query roles, candidate strata, the grading mechanics on rectangular candidate subsets, the paired-difference statistics, and the guardrails that make a held-context number interpretable rather than leaked.

Sources: [loco.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/loco.py#L1-L17), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L1-L12)

## The LOCO Fold: Withholding an Entire Cell Context

The defining move of this protocol is the unit of held-out data. Identity-level cross-validation withholds rows; the LOCO fold withholds a *context*: in each of four folds, the held context's responses are invisible to every predictor because the training pool is built only from the other three contexts. Inside the held context there is deliberately **no hash split** — the held context contributes no training row at all, so nothing it is graded on could ever have fitted the predictor, and splitting it further would only discard half of its queries. Outside the anchor, every usable identity of a non-anchor context is both a potential training row (in folds where it trains) and a query (in its own fold).

Sources: [contexts.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contexts.py#L8-L16), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L76-L95)

Each fold is not a single comparison but a scaling experiment. The `designs` function enumerates **seven atlas designs** per fold — the three single training contexts, the three pairs, and the pooled triple — all fitted under one unchanged recipe with no context feature anywhere. Crucially, the evaluation population is fixed per fold: `SEEN_CANDIDATE` is defined against the *full* three-context training set rather than against each design, so a one-context design and a three-context design are graded on exactly the same candidates; each design additionally records the fraction of each stratum it actually supervised, which is the number that would otherwise hide inside a moving population.

Sources: [loco.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/loco.py#L4-L14), [loco.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/loco.py#L44-L49)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Train["Training pool — the other three contexts"]
        R["Fit rows only: candidate features + consensus responses"]
    end
    subgraph Held["Held context — zero training influence"]
        Q["Eligible queries: usable and eligible identities"]
        P["Candidate pool: every usable identity"]
    end
    R -->|"WeightedRidgePath fit"| V1["V1 design predicted effects"]
    V1 --> F["effect_cosine fused with frozen BASE scores"]
    P --> F
    F --> M["Per-stratum metrics: MBRU, Mean at B, HighValueCount at B"]
    Q --> M
    B["Frozen CLEAN_BASE arm"] --> M
    O["ORACLE and RANDOM reference arms"] --> M
    M --> S["Paired medians + cluster bootstrap per stratum"]
```

A design whose training pool cannot support the frozen basis rank is **recorded, not raised**: it is skipped with a machine-readable reason (`usable_rows`, `basis_rank`), because a design that cannot support the frozen rank is a fact about the atlas, and silently lowering the rank would turn it into a different method and void the comparison.

Sources: [loco.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/loco.py#L110-L121)

## Who May Train on What: Per-Context Roles and the Sealed Anchor

The one asymmetry in the protocol is the **anchor**, K562, because the frozen `CLEAN_BASE` ranker used as the reference arm in *every* fold was trained on K562's `G_fit` identities. The anchor therefore keeps an internal role structure — train on `G_fit`, query on `G_select` — so the base is never evaluated in-sample, while the three new contexts keep the undivided rule. `G_select` is a selection split and not a blind one, so K562 absolute numbers are optimistic for the base; the protocol responds by reporting K562 only through **paired differences under that same base**, and by excluding the anchor's `G_fit` identities from its evaluation population.

| Context | Training rows (`TRAIN_RULE`) | Evaluation queries (`QUERY_RULE`) | Protocol consequence |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **K562** (anchor) | usable identities in the anchor `G_fit` role | usable, `QUERY_ELIGIBILITY_V1`-eligible identities in the `G_select` role | `G_check` sealed and dropped; base trained here, so only paired deltas are meaningful |
| **RPE1** | every usable identity | every usable and eligible identity | no internal split; queried in its own fold |
| **HepG2** | every usable identity | every usable and eligible identity | no internal split; queried in its own fold |
| **Jurkat** | every usable identity | every usable and eligible identity | no internal split; queried in its own fold |

Sources: [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L76-L95), [contexts.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contexts.py#L27-L29)

The anchor is loaded from frozen assets, never rebuilt — the anchor lock forbids it. `load_anchor` enforces the seal mechanically: it raises `RuntimeError` if any `G_check` identity would become reachable through the train or query role indices, and `G_check` rows are then physically dropped from every array the programme can touch. A protocol test pins the rule down: only the anchor may restrict which identities may train or be queried, and any future edit that reintroduces a split for RPE1, HepG2 or Jurkat will fail pytest and thus be forced to be a deliberate contract change.

Sources: [contexts.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contexts.py#L88-L135), [test_protocol.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/test_protocol.py#L34-L42)

The gene axis is frozen once, before any model runs: `G_4`, the sorted intersection of the four measured axes. The historical K562 result keeps its own 8248-gene axis and is not recomputed — the four-context programme is a separate experiment on `G_4`.

Sources: [contexts.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contexts.py#L137-L142), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L28-L32)

## Candidate Strata: Context Transfer versus Candidate Transfer

The protocol insists that two things called "generalization" are **never collapsed into one number**. A candidate whose response was measured in some training context had its own effect supervised, so evaluating it in the held context isolates whether the *context* mapping transfers. A candidate no training context ever measured additionally tests whether the *candidate* mapping transfers. Stratum membership is a property of **which identities were measured where** — it never depends on a score, so the partition cannot be gamed by a model's own behaviour.

| Stratum | Membership rule | Question it isolates |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `ALL` | every usable identity of the held context | overall held-context performance |
| `SEEN_CANDIDATE` | response measured in at least one training context | context transfer only |
| `UNSEEN_CANDIDATE` | measured in no training context | context transfer + candidate-mapping transfer |
| `COMMON4` | usable in all four contexts | the only population on which a context residual can be estimated at all |

Sources: [overlap.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/overlap.py#L1-L13), [overlap.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/overlap.py#L35-L40)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    ALL["ALL: every usable identity of the held context"] --> SEEN["SEEN_CANDIDATE: measured in a training context — isolates context transfer"]
    ALL --> UNSEEN["UNSEEN_CANDIDATE: measured nowhere in training — adds candidate-mapping transfer"]
    ALL --> C4["COMMON4: usable in all four contexts — required for context-residual estimation"]
    SEEN -.->|"disjoint by construction"| UNSEEN
```

The masks are computed from data alone by `fold_strata`, alongside a recorded overlap matrix (pairwise Jaccard, and how many identities are measured in exactly *k* contexts) that documents how much supervised material each fold actually shares.

Sources: [overlap.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/overlap.py#L21-L32), [overlap.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/overlap.py#L43-L58), [overlap.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/overlap.py#L73-L80)

## Grading Mechanics on a Held Context

Everything a fold reads is assembled **once per context**, not per arm: the frozen base scores, the graded utility, the candidate knowledge features and the response arrays live in a `ContextPack`. The rationale is experimental control — if base scores or utility were rebuilt per arm, a difference between two arms could come from a rebuild rather than from the arm itself.

Sources: [harness.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/harness.py#L1-L8), [harness.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/harness.py#L28-L45)

Two conventions in the pack deserve attention. First, utility is graded **cross-view**: a query scored under view *v* is graded by the responses of the batch-disjoint view *1−v*, so even in-context grading uses independently measured outcomes (the A/B batch-disjoint views are inherited verbatim from the frozen measurement lock). Second, the pack asserts every evaluation query sits inside its own context's candidate pool and records its `self_positions` index, which is what makes self-exclusion possible during ranking.

Sources: [evaluate.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L41-L46), [harness.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/harness.py#L82-L124), [split.py](src/gene_open_inverse/measurement_v2_quad/split.py#L34-L44)

The evaluator then restricts to a stratum, which makes the score and utility matrices **rectangular**: the query axis stays the held context's eligible queries while the candidate axis shrinks to the stratum. This is the mechanism that separates candidate generalization from context generalization. The consequence is deliberate and important: restricting the pool also moves the per-query random and oracle references, because within a stratum the achievable ceiling is that stratum's own ceiling — so an absolute number from one stratum is not comparable to another's, and **only paired differences between arms inside one stratum** are interpreted. A stratum holding no more candidates than the largest frozen budget is skipped outright rather than graded.

Sources: [evaluate.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L1-L17), [evaluate.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L148-L174)

> [!TIP]
> Self-exclusion must survive the restriction: when a stratum does not contain its own query, the excluded index passed to the frozen `stable_order` is `None`, never `-1` — the frozen sorter would read `-1` as "the last candidate" and silently delete a real, possibly top-utility, candidate from every ordering. `test_05` exists precisely because this defect looks like a valid result.

Sources: [evaluate.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L12-L17), [evaluate.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L105-L133), [test_protocol.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/test_protocol.py#L66-L78)

Candidate effects are scored as `cos(d_q, r_hat_c)` — cosine between the query's measured view-response direction and the predicted effect, with candidates that received no prediction (e.g. all knowledge modalities missing) scored at exactly zero — and then fused with the base arm by the frozen additive rule: per-query-row z-scores at unit weight, standardized over **the whole scored pool** by default (the published runs' convention). An explicit `standardize_over` option exists for subpool-fair fusion, returning 0.0 outside the subset so a subset ranking can never depend on what lies outside it.

Sources: [evaluate.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L47-L54), [evaluate.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L81-L102), [harness.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/harness.py#L140-L143)

## Reference Arms and the Paired-Difference Statistic

Every fold grades the same four kinds of arm on every stratum. The frozen evaluation contract fixes the statistic: the **median of paired per-row differences** (mean reported beside it), with cluster bootstrap over the query gene — 10,000 replicates at seed 20260916 — and budgets of 10/20/50 with BU@20 as the primary headline metric.

| Arm | Score construction | Role in the protocol |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `BASE` | frozen K562 `CLEAN_BASE` scorer, run unchanged on `G_4` values embedded on the anchor axis | fixed reference for every context and every fold; never retrained, never adapted, never told which context it sees |
| `RANDOM` | per-fold seeded Gaussian scores | diagnostic only, never a comparison of record; `BASE − RANDOM` reveals whether the base transfers to an unseen context at all |
| `ORACLE` | the graded utility itself | per-stratum ceiling; `test_06` verifies its MBRU equals 1.0 |
| `V1[design]` | frozen fusion of `BASE` with the effect cosine of a ridge predictor trained on one atlas design | the comparison of record; `delta_MBRU_effect_minus_base` is the pre-registered scaling quantity |
| `V2` | `V1` plus a low-rank context residual fitted on training-context source states only | primary `V2` vs `V1` comparison; degenerates to `V1` when context carries nothing |

Sources: [evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L7-L18), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L42-L52), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L116-L125), [loco.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/loco.py#L100-L107)

One naming nuance matters for cross-reading the codebase: the paper-level contract designates `BU@20` as primary and retires `MBRU` from headline tables, yet the four-context protocol's pre-registered scaling quantity is `delta_MBRU_effect_minus_base`, and the sealed anchor is reported on its pre-registered MBRU only. These are consistent levels of the protocol: MBRU is the per-row paired vehicle inside the four-context scaling analysis, while BU@B-style budgets carry the paper's primary claims — the metric families themselves are covered in [Ranking Metrics: BU@B, MU@B, PHR@B](8-ranking-metrics-buatb-muatb-phratb).

Sources: [evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/evaluation_contract_v1/contract.py#L10-L24), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L116-L119)

The fold record computes three paired families per stratum: each arm against `BASE`, `BASE` against `RANDOM` (the base-transfer diagnostic), and the pooled-triple design against each smaller design (the atlas-scaling delta). Each paired entry is the median difference plus the cluster bootstrap and the fraction of queries improved. Because both measurement views are pooled per query, query counts in a stratum block are double the eligible-query count.

Sources: [evaluate.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L140-L145), [loco.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/loco.py#L141-L156)

## The Deployment Firewall: What a Held-Context Run May Never See

The protocol separates what a held-context number *means* from what the run may *consume* via an explicit deployment firewall: the only legal inputs are candidate static knowledge and the source/control state; forbidden inputs are the candidate perturbed state, the target perturbation outcome, and — the one that matters on this page — the **held-context candidate response**. The fold record self-documents its compliance with two boolean flags written into the JSON output itself: `read_anchor_G_check: False` and `context_feature_given_to_any_model: False`.

| Guardrail | Enforcement mechanism |
| :--- | :--- |
| Held-context responses never enter inference features | `FORBIDDEN_INPUTS` list; predictors consume only static knowledge features + training-context responses |
| Anchor `G_check` sealed | `ANCHOR_G_CHECK_IS_SEALED`; `load_anchor` raises if a sealed identity becomes reachable; rows dropped from all arrays |
| No context identity leaked to V1 | `context_feature_given_to_any_model: False` recorded in the fold JSON |
| Base ranker frozen | loaded read-only from the lock checkpoint in `load_base_model`; no training code path exists in the harness |
| Symmetric embedding | every context, anchor included, is embedded onto the anchor's 8248-gene axis with zeros elsewhere, so the base sees the same number of informative coordinates everywhere |

Sources: [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L158-L165), [loco.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/loco.py#L78-L91), [harness.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/harness.py#L59-L79)

The embedding symmetry is worth pausing on: leaving K562 on its full 8248 genes while the new contexts carry only the `G_4` intersection would make the base stronger in one context for a reason unrelated to the question being asked, so the protocol embeds every context identically and declares the residual asymmetry — the base was *trained* on K562 — rather than correcting it, which makes the K562 fold's effect-minus-base delta harder, not easier.

Sources: [harness.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/harness.py#L59-L69), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L34-L43)

For the context-conditioned V2 arm, the firewall holds too: the context representation `P_ctx` is fitted on **training-context source states only** — control pseudobulks, no perturbed cell — and the penalty for the residual's single linear map is selected by leave-one-training-context-out *inside the three training contexts*, so the held context is absent from every fitting step.

Sources: [v2.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/v2.py#L2-L30), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L127-L146)

## Attribution Controls Inside the Fold

Because the pooled triple has both more rows and more contexts, a pooled win is uninterpretable on its own — this is stated as the reason the mission exists (Q2). Inside the same protocol the row-budget rule is pre-registered: each arm trains on exactly the largest budget every comparable single-context design can meet, computed from row counts alone and never from a model result, with rows split evenly across a design's contexts; five match seeds are fixed in the contract and are never raised after seeing a result. A design too small for the frozen rank is recorded as skipped rather than silently re-ranked.

Sources: [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L4-L13), [contract.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L116-L125), [matched.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/matched.py#L1-L21), [matched.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/matched.py#L43-L59)

## Protocol Verification and Positive Controls

The protocol test suite targets defects that would otherwise masquerade as results: a quarter assignment that is not a refinement of the frozen A/B split, a weighted ridge that quietly disagrees with the frozen solver, a self-exclusion that deletes the wrong candidate, strata whose halves overlap (`SEEN ∪ UNSEEN = ALL`, empty intersection, `COMMON4 ⊆ ALL`), and a fusion step that reorders a row it should not. The full suite is described in [Protocol Test Suite](24-protocol-test-suite).

Sources: [test_protocol.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/test_protocol.py#L1-L9), [test_protocol.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/test_protocol.py#L92-L97)

Complementing the negative tests, `identifiability.py` runs a **positive control** on the protocol itself: if a held-context residual of exactly the pre-registered V2 form were planted in synthetic data, could this training, regularization and selection pipeline recover it from three training contexts? Without that answer, a real `V2 − V1 ≤ 0` would be ambiguous between "context carries nothing" and "three contexts cannot identify the model" — and the share curve (0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50) is an identifiability curve, not a search.

Sources: [identifiability.py](src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/identifiability.py#L1-L31)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    FC["four_context_v1.contract: frozen constants"] --> HN
    CX["contexts.py: uniform Context objects"] --> HN["harness.py: ContextPack per context"]
    CB["final_clean_model_v1: frozen CLEAN_BASE"] --> HN
    HN --> LOCO["loco.py: fold driver"]
    OV["overlap.py: strata masks"] --> LOCO
    PDs["predictors.py: WeightedRidgePath"] --> LOCO
    EV["evaluate.py: stratum metrics, fuse, paired"] --> LOCO
    MT["matched.py: row-matched controls"] --> EV
    V2m["v2.py: context residual on V1"] --> EV
    LOCO --> OUT["Fold JSON record + common4.json"]
```

## Where This Fits in the Catalog

The protocol page sits between the metric definitions and their interpretation. Read [Ranking Metrics: BU@B, MU@B, PHR@B](8-ranking-metrics-buatb-muatb-phratb) for the graded quantities this harness consumes, then [Decision Routes: Retrieval versus Prediction](10-decision-routes-retrieval-versus-prediction) for how held-context arms translate into deployment choices; [Four-Context Data Contracts](17-four-context-data-contracts) documents how each context is built to satisfy the qualification gate before any fold runs, [Leakage Prevention and Identity-Level Cross-Validation](21-leakage-prevention-and-identity-level-cross-validation) covers the identity-level regime that LOCO deliberately replaces at the context level, and [Key Benchmark Findings](26-key-benchmark-findings) reports the numbers this protocol produced.


# Decision Routes: Retrieval versus Prediction



Every intervention-design problem in VCDesign asks the same question — rank a candidate pool and commit an experimental budget $B$ — but two distinct scoring families can fill the score matrix that the ranking consumes. This page defines the two **decision routes**: *direct response-profile retrieval*, which uses a candidate's measured response as its score, and *predicted-effect scoring*, the VCDesign-CED route, which synthesizes a score from static knowledge alone. It covers where each route is legal, how both converge on one shared decision interface, and how the evaluation harness keeps them exactly comparable.

## One Interface, Two Scoring Families

Both routes emit the same artifact: a `[queries × pool]` float matrix, one score per query-candidate pair. The grader never learns which route produced a matrix — `evaluate_arms` accepts any `score_by_arm` dictionary and runs every arm through the identical `stratum_metrics` pipeline (stable ordering, self-exclusion, `query_references`, budget prefix metrics). The evaluator's module docstring states the comparability rule directly: restricting the pool moves each stratum's own random and oracle references, so **only paired differences between arms inside one stratum are interpretable** — an absolute number from one stratum is never comparable to another's. This is what makes a retrieval arm and a prediction arm legitimately face each other in one table: they are two columns of the same grading contract, not two different experiments.

Sources: [evaluate.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L1-L17), [evaluate.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L152-L182)

The decision interface itself is defined by the frozen four-context contract: a candidate pool, a budget set, and outcome-based grading. The README's "Choose the information regime" table frames the route choice as the only genuinely open decision: *measured candidate responses available* → direct response-profile retrieval; *candidate responses unavailable* → VCDesign-CED predicted-effect scoring. Both routes feed "the same downstream decision interface: a candidate pool, an experimental budget, and outcome-based evaluation."

Sources: [contract.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L111-L115), [README.md](/README.md#L72-L81)

## The Retrieval Route: Measured Responses as the Score

Retrieval scores a candidate by the geometric alignment between what the query wants and what the candidate measurably did. The measured quantity is the **consensus response** `r̄_c` — `consensus()` averages the two batch-disjoint measurement views into one response direction per candidate. Grading itself follows the anchor convention implemented in `cross_view_utility`: a query measured in view $v$ is graded by view $1-v$ responses, so the graded utility is literally a cross-view response cosine. This is why the **ORACLE arm** (`oracle_scores`, which ranks by the graded utility itself) represents the retrieval family's ceiling: it achieves perfect alignment with the grading function by reading the very responses the firewall forbids at deployment time. It is a reference bound, not a deployable route.

Sources: [evaluate.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L32-L54), [evaluate.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L140-L142), [loco.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/loco.py#L105-L107)

Legality is a function of *where* the responses came from. The deployment firewall in the frozen contract lists three `FORBIDDEN_INPUTS` — the candidate's perturbed state, the target perturbation outcome, and the **held-context candidate response**. Retrieval that reads responses measured in *other* training contexts is legal and deployable; retrieval that reads the held context's own measurements is the oracle. The manuscript's headline comparison quantifies the legal version: when candidate responses have been measured in other contexts, direct profile retrieval scores pooled BU@20 `0.675` against VCDesign-CED's `0.508`.

Sources: [contract.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L163-L169), [README.md](/README.md#L82-L90)

## The Prediction Route: VCDesign-CED

The prediction route assembles its score from two branches that are then fused. The **base branch** is the frozen `CLEAN_BASE` scorer: loaded read-only by `load_base_model`, never retrained, never told which context it is looking at — it scores source-to-goal alignment over candidate static knowledge (STRING + MAP-KG descriptors) embedded on the anchor gene axis. The **effect branch** is the CED predictor's output, `r̂_c = B ẑ_c`, reconstructed from the response basis and scored against the query direction by `effect_cosine` — with the hard rule that a candidate having no predicted effect scores exactly zero, and `EffectPredictor.effect` zeroes out any candidate lacking a legal knowledge modality. `effect_arms` glues the two per measurement view: `fuse(pack.base[view], ev.effect_cosine(pack.query_responses, effect, view))`.

Sources: [harness.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/harness.py#L74-L82), [harness.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/harness.py#L157-L160), [predictors.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/predictors.py#L83-L87)

The fusion itself is deliberately frozen: `fuse()` performs row-wise z-score standardization of each branch, adds them at unit weight β=1.0 with no fitted coefficient. By default each branch is standardized over **every column of the pool it is given** — the published runs standardize over the whole scored pool, not the evaluated subset. An optional `standardize_over` mask restricts standardization to a column subset and returns 0.0 elsewhere, making those columns ungradable.

Sources: [evaluate.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L82-L104), [evaluate.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L57-L60)

> [!TIP]
> Route architecture at a glance — both branches of the prediction route and the retrieval route terminate in the same `[queries × pool]` matrix and the same grader:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Inputs["Decision-time inputs"]
        S["source / control state"]
        K["STRING + MAP-KG static knowledge"]
        R["measured responses r̄_c<br/>(other contexts only)"]
    end
    S --> BASE["frozen CLEAN_BASE scorer<br/>(never retrained)"]
    K --> BASE
    K --> CED["CED ridge effect predictor<br/>r̂_c = B ẑ_c<br/>(no modality ⇒ zero)"]
    R -->|"retrieval route"| RET["cross-view response cosine"]
    BASE --> FUSE["fuse(): row_z(base) + β·row_z(effect)"]
    CED --> ECOS["effect_cosine: cos(d_q, r̂_c)"]
    ECOS --> FUSE
    FUSE --> SCORE["VCDesign-CED score matrix"]
    RET --> RSCORE["Retrieval score matrix"]
    RSCORE --> GRADER
    SCORE --> GRADER["evaluate_arms → stratum_metrics<br/>MBRU · Mean@B · HighValueCount@B"]
```

Prerequisite for reading this diagram: a *query direction* $d_q$ is the query's view-`v` unit-normalized response; both routes reduce to cosines against directions — measured (`r̄_c`) versus predicted (`r̂_c`) — added to a base alignment score only in the prediction route.

## When Each Route Applies: The Decision Rule

The route choice is dictated entirely by the candidate's measurement status at decision time, and the manuscript's numbers bound what each choice is worth:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Decision request: source-to-target transition, budget B"] --> B{"Candidate response<br/>measured anywhere?"}
    B -->|"Yes, in training contexts"| C["Route: retrieval<br/>pooled BU@20 = 0.675<br/>beats prediction 0.508"]
    B -->|"No — response unseen"| D["Retrieval undefined;<br/>prediction route only"]
    D --> E{"Candidate has ≥1<br/>knowledge modality?"}
    E -->|"Yes"| F["VCDesign-CED fusion<br/>masked-condition gain vs base: +0.0492 BU@20"]
    E -->|"No"| G["Effect branch = 0;<br/>frozen all-missing behavior"]
```

| Decision situation | Legal route | Evidence of record |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Response measured in other contexts | Retrieval **or** prediction; retrieval wins | Pooled BU@20 `0.675` (retrieval) vs `0.508` (CED) |
| Response never measured | Prediction only | Masked-condition paired gain `+0.0492` BU@20 over the same base scorer; `1.11` more top-5% candidates among 20 selections |
| No knowledge modality present | Prediction with zeroed effect branch | Frozen all-missing score defined by the protocol |

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L72-L90), [predictors.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/predictors.py#L83-L87)

Note that the protocol's own quantity of record is always expressed *within* the prediction route: `PRIMARY_QUANTITY = "delta_MBRU_effect_minus_base"` — the mission measures whether the effect branch improves the base, judged on "budgeted intervention design utility, never response reconstruction." The retrieval-versus-prediction question is a separate, deployment-facing comparison layered on top of this primary quantity.

Sources: [contract.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/open_vocab_generalization_v1/contract.py#L84-L87)

## The Arm Taxonomy: Routes as Experimental Arms

The harness never hard-codes a route; it instantiates each route (and each route's controls) as a named **arm** whose value is the shared `[queries × pool]` score matrix. Reading the arm table is reading the route system:

| Arm | Route family | Score source | Experimental role | Code anchor |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `BASE` | neither — reference | frozen `CLEAN_BASE` alone | transfer baseline every delta is measured against | [loco.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/loco.py#L105-L107) |
| `RANDOM` | none — diagnostic | seeded Gaussian | keeps `BASE` interpretable where the base never trained | [loco.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/loco.py#L101-L106) |
| `V1[design]` | prediction | `effect_arms(pack, effect)` per atlas design | CED at fixed recipe across 7 atlas designs | [loco.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/loco.py#L122-L125) |
| `V2` | prediction (context-conditioned) | V1 + low-rank context residual | does context conditioning help | [contract.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/contract.py#L118-L120) |
| `EFFECT_SEEN` | prediction | fusion with full-atlas predictor | response-exposed prediction | [masking.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/open_vocab_generalization_v1/masking.py#L333-L336) |
| `EFFECT_MASKED` | prediction | fusion with crossfit masked predictor | response-unseen prediction — the deployment condition | [masking.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/open_vocab_generalization_v1/masking.py#L352-L355) |
| `EFFECT_SIZE_CONTROL` | prediction | fusion with next-fold predictor | separates "never measured" from "smaller atlas" | [masking.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/open_vocab_generalization_v1/masking.py#L206-L215) |
| `ORACLE` | retrieval ceiling | the graded utility itself | upper bound; not deployable | [evaluate.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L140-L142) |

The arm assembly is deliberately factored so that route differences cannot be confounded with rebuild differences: the base ranker, candidate features, and graded utility are computed **once per context** in the `ContextPack` and reused by every arm and every atlas size — "if they were rebuilt per arm, a difference between two arms could come from a rebuild rather than from the arm."

Sources: [harness.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/harness.py#L1-L8), [harness.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/harness.py#L28-L46)

> [!TIP]
> The masked arm's score columns are *not* zeroed outside the eligible set. `_crossfit` copies the seen arm's prediction into ineligible columns, because the frozen fusion standardizes each row over the whole pool before evaluation restricts it — filling those columns with zeros would hand the masked arm a different effective fusion weight and turn the exposure contrast into a fusion artifact.

Sources: [masking.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/open_vocab_generalization_v1/masking.py#L279-L296)

## Comparability Guarantees Across Routes

Three mechanisms guarantee that a retrieval number and a prediction number in the same table mean the same thing. **First**, identical grading: every arm passes through `stratum_metrics`, where self-exclusion survives pool restriction — the excluded index is recorded as `None` rather than `-1`, because the frozen `stable_order` would read `-1` as the last candidate and silently delete a real one. **Second**, exposure manipulations refit everything they legally touch: `masked_training_pool` removes a candidate's rows *by identity in every named context at once*, and the response basis and ridge are rebuilt inside the masked pool — reusing the seen arm's basis would leak masked responses through the very object the protocol says must be rebuilt. **Third**, stratification is shared: `SEEN_CANDIDATE` / `UNSEEN_CANDIDATE` masks are defined against the full training set rather than per design, so arms are graded on the same candidates, and paired statistics (`paired`, cluster bootstrap) are computed within-stratum.

Sources: [evaluate.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/evaluate.py#L13-L16), [masking.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/open_vocab_generalization_v1/masking.py#L65-L86), [masking.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/open_vocab_generalization_v1/masking.py#L1-L30), [loco.py](/src/gene_open_inverse/four_context_v1/loco.py#L8-L14)

> [!TIP]
> The route choice has a sharp boundary in the code: any candidate with a measured response *somewhere* can be served by retrieval; any candidate without one falls to prediction, where the all-missing case degenerates gracefully to the base score because the zeroed effect branch contributes a constant row to the z-scored sum.

## Reading Progression

This page sits at the hinge between the evaluation framework and the distillation pipeline. For the grading machinery both routes feed, see [Ranking Metrics: BU@B, MU@B, PHR@B](8-ranking-metrics-buatb-muatb-phratb) and [Held-Out Context Evaluation Protocol](9-held-out-context-evaluation-protocol). For how the prediction route's effect branch is built, continue to [Response Basis Construction](11-response-basis-construction) and [Ridge Effect Predictor](12-ridge-effect-predictor); for the fusion mechanics and β selection, see [Score Fusion and Beta Selection](14-score-fusion-and-beta-selection); for the base branch, see [Final Clean Base Scorer](15-final-clean-base-scorer). For the experiment that quantifies the prediction route's value under response absence, see [Response Masking and Open-Vocabulary Analyses](18-response-masking-and-open-vocabulary-analyses).

# Response Basis Construction



This page documents how the Candidate Effect Distillation (CED) pipeline builds its linear substrate: the **measured response target** and the **response basis `B`**.
